title: LeAnn Rimes shares naked hot tub photo with Eddie Cibrian on road trip from California to Nashville
summary: LeAnn Rimes shared a naked hot tub photo with Eddie Cibrian during their cross-country road trip from California back to Nashville on Instagram.
story: The "Blue" singer said she and Cibrian love each other and can be stupid together.
LeAnn Rimes is spending her road trip from California back home to Nashville naked in a hot tub with her husband, Eddie Cibrian.

On Tuesday, Rimes took to Instagram to document their journey. In the carousel of images, the singer and actress shared a photo at the end of her post, taken from behind. Cibrian had his arm around her while she sat naked in the hot tub, taking in the scenic view.
"The last picture is what its ALL about. @leannrimes ❤️," one user commented, referencing the hot tub photo. Another added, "The last photo with you and @eddiecibrian just warms my heart!"
LeAnn Rimes and Eddie Cibrian cuddled in the hot tub in one image the singer shared to her Instagram page. (LeAnn Rimes/Instagram)

"there were questionable roadside sightings, car karaoke, a LOT of gas station potty breaks, incredible food and a few moments that probably should’ve stayed off camera… but didn’t."
LEANN RIMES POSES IN RED BIKINI IN CABO, SHARES EMOTIONAL MESSAGE ABOUT 'HEART-WRENCHING' FAMILY ISSUES
The "Blue" singer included a link to her substack, which had a more in-depth write-up of their road trip.
Rimes and Cibrian enjoyed the hot tub on their road trip from California to Nashville. (Monica Schipper/Getty Images)

Eddie Cibrian and LeAnn Rimes have been married since 2011. (Jacob Andrzejczak/Getty Images for MGM Resorts International)

title: Ella Langley joins music royalty with 'insane' milestone for 'Choosin' Texas'
summary: Ella Langley's "Choosin' Texas" tied a Billboard Hot 100 record with 14 weeks at No. 1, matching Mariah Carey and Whitney Houston among non-holiday titles by women.
story: Ella Langley discusses releasing a series of singles and building momentum toward her sophomore album while at the 2026 iHeartRadio Music Awards.
Ella Langley likely has a smile written on her face.
Her "Choosin' Texas" anthem placed at No. 1 on the Billboard Hot 100 charts, its 14th week at the top, tying a record with two iconic hits.
Langley, 27, called the career milestone "insane" in a post shared on Instagram stories shortly after earning the spot.
ELLA LANGLEY SUFFERS WARDROBE MALFUNCTION WHILE OPENING FOR MORGAN WALLEN IN BALTIMORE
Ella Langley topped the Billboard Hot 100 charts for the 14th week in a row with her "Choosin' Texas" anthem. (John Schearer)

The country ballad first topped the Hot 100 in February and now matches Mariah Carey's "We Belong Together" and Whitney Houston's "I Will Always Love You" for most weeks at No. 1 among non-holiday titles by women with no male-billed acts.
In addition, "Choosing Texas" ties Carey's "All I Want for Christmas Is You" for second-longest ranking hit.
Ella Langley celebrated her 14th week at the top of the Billboard 100 charts. (Instagram/Ella Langley)
Langley broke onto the country music scene nearly a decade ago and released her debut studio album, "Hungover," in 2024.
MORGAN WALLEN AND ELLA LANGLEY HOLD THE TOP TWO ALBUM SPOTS IN AMERICA FOR FIRST HALF OF 2026
The catalog brought her immediate accolades with hits, including "You Look Like You Love Me" and "Weren't for the Wind" both reaching No. 1 on country charts.
Her sophomore release, "Dandelion," debuted at No. 1 on the Billboard Hot 200 upon its release in April.
Ella Langley released her debut studio album in 2024. (Rich Polk/Billboard)
"Choosin' Texas" not only capped the Billboard Hot 100, but recently earned Langley the title of first female artist to simultaneously top the Hot 100, Hot Country Songs and Country Airplay charts.
MIRANDA LAMBERT DELIVERS STRAIGHT-SHOOTING ADVICE TO RISING COUNTRY STAR IN SURPRISE BATHROOM ENCOUNTER
The "Dandelion" title was inspired by the sturdy plant which is known to withstand challenging environments.

"I learned that dandelion tea is actually a natural detox for the liver," Ella told Billboard ahead of the release. "So, a record called ‘Dandelion’ after a record called hungover made all the sense in the world to me.
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR THE ENTERTAINMENT NEWSLETTER
Ella Langley has become one of country music's fastest-rising stars. (Jason Kempin/Getty Images)
LIKE WHAT YOU'RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE ENTERTAINMENT NEWS

"I’ve never poured more of myself into a project, into a song, into an idea, and it’s fallen out so beautifully. It’s about learning yourself, making mistakes and realizing that it’s all just part of life.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

"I want this record to be something that fans can relate to but also something they want to get up and dance to at the same time. To me, this record feels like fireflies in the summertime. It feels like windows down on a red dirt road. It feels like the best kind of Sunday afternoon. It feels like those days I remember as a kid where it felt like there weren’t enough hours in the day. This record is really a love letter to that."
Langley served as executive producer on the album and co-wrote "Choosin' Texas" alongside Miranda Lambert, Luke Dick and JoyBeth Taylor.

Kaylee Hottle has died, Fox News Digital can confirm.

title: Shania Twain says she's finally 'getting it right' in her 60s after starting life ‘on the tough side’
summary: Shania Twain opened up about how childhood poverty, stage fright and a Lyme disease battle shaped her journey to finding peace in her 60s.
story: Shania Twain told Fox News Digital at the 2024 Peoples Choice Country Awards that shes embracing the "evolution of country music."
Shania Twain is looking back on her long journey from an impoverished childhood in rural Canada to international superstardom and finally coming to terms with her past in her 60s.
During a recent interview with "CBS Mornings," the 60-year-old singer opened up about her difficult upbringing and how she has gained a new outlook later in life.
"I started life out a little bit on the tough side," Twain said. "In my 60s now, I feel like I've really gotten it, or I'm just now getting all of that right."
Shania Twain opened up about how she feels she is finally "getting it right" in her 60s. (Matthew Baker/Getty Images for ABA)
When asked by CBS correspondent Seth Doane about why her 60s had given her that perspective, Twain had a simple answer.
SHANIA TWAIN'S LIQUID DIET HELPS HER AVOID A ‘NIGHTMARE’ CONCERT MISHAP

"You know what it is? It's called time," she said. "I'd love to have been able to get it right in my 50s, but I just – that wasn't enough time. I needed to be in my 60s to start getting it right, you know?"

Born Eilleen Regina Edwards in Windsor, Ontario, Twain was raised in the small town of Timmins by her mother, Sharon, and adoptive father Jerry Twain after her biological parents divorced when she was 2 years old.
Twain spoke candidly about starting life "on the tough side." (Mathew Tsang/Getty Images)
TAYLOR HICKS CREDITS FAITH AND BLUE-COLLAR BIRMINGHAM ROOTS FOR KEEPING HIM GROUNDED AFTER 'AMERICAN IDOL' WIN
Twain's family struggled financially, and the singer has spoken candidly about growing up in poverty and witnessing domestic abuse at home.
While speaking with "CBS Mornings," Twain recalled that she was forced to grow up quickly, taking on burdens that far exceeded those of a typical child.

"When I was younger, I was so over-responsible for the household," she remembered. "My mother was depressed a lot of the time. She spent a lot of her days in bed. She lived off coffee and cigarettes that I would bring her in bed just to see if she was still alive."
VANILLA ICE SAYS HE NEARLY JOINED THE ‘27 CLUB’ BEFORE QUITTING DRUGS FOR GOOD
"There was a lot of violence in the house," Twain added. "And we didn't eat well a lot of the times. We weren't clothed properly a lot of the time."
The singer began performing at bars when she was just 8 to help support her family. (Robert Smith/Patrick McMullan via Getty Images)
Long before becoming one of country music's biggest stars, Twain performed in bars as a child to help support her family, including her mother, stepfather and four siblings.
The singer shared that her early performing years led her to develop stage fright, which would plague her for most of her career regardless of her audience size.

"The amount of people is not necessarily what affected me over the years with stage fright," Twain said. "It was starting so young in bars that were, you know, I was 8 years old, and the bars were smoky, and everyone was intoxicated. I don't know what I'm actually singing about, because I'm singing about divorce, and I'm eight."
Twain explained that she did not realize how deeply those experiences had shaped her until much later in life.

"This was just an uncomfortable place to be as a child, and I carried that with me," she said. "And only in my 50s, I finally just said, 'Whoa. I've got my voice. I have an audience. I have everything to just celebrate.' And the fear just dropped away."
Twain explained that her early years as a child performer led her to have stage fright for decades. (Jim Spellman/WireImage)

Twain's challenges did not end with her difficult childhood. In 1987, when she was 22, her mother and stepfather were killed in a car accident. While both Twain and her older sister Jill were already adults, their three younger siblings, including sister Carrie-Ann and brothers Mark and Darry, were underage and needed a legal guardian.

At the time, Twain was trying to establish herself as a singer-songwriter after moving to Toronto to pursue music. However, Twain put her career on hold and moved back to Ontario to care for her younger siblings.
During a 2023 appearance on "The Drew Barrymore Show," Twain recalled the difficulties that she faced after becoming her siblings' primary caregiver.
GOLDIE HAWN THINKS KIDS LACK 'GRIT' FROM TOO MUCH SCREEN TIME, NOT ENOUGH REAL-WORLD PROBLEM SOLVING

"That was a different type of parenting because now there was nobody to blame because now they’re gone," she said. "All of a sudden, I’m responsible for making decisions about my parents’ mortgage. I didn’t know they had a mortgage, I didn’t know what it was, I didn’t know anything about how they ran their business or debts or insurance. I had to learn overnight. My parents died — three days later I’m in lawyer’s offices and insurance company offices."
Twain told "CBS Mornings" that with the benefit of time, she is now able to look back on those experiences with gratitude instead of focusing solely on the hardship.
The singer became her three younger siblings' primary caregiver after their parents died in a car accident. (Getty Images)

"When I reflect back on those times, I'm reflecting on them from where I am now, which is a very good place," Twain said. "Like, I made it out of there. It's like, 'Whoa, I'm just celebrating all of that.' And what makes me feel so accomplished, is staying connected to where I came from. It's the contrast that makes it feel so good."

After her siblings were older and living independently, Twain finally turned her attention back to her own dreams. In 1991, she moved to Nashville and signed a recording deal with the legendary country music label Mercury Nashville.

Twain's breakthrough came in 1995 with the release of her Grammy-winning sophomore album, "The Woman in Me." Two years later, she skyrocketed to global fame with "Come On Over," the best-selling album by a female artist of all time.
JANE SEYMOUR, 75, SHARES HOW SHE APPROACHES AGING WITH VITALITY: 'BEST I CAN BE'
Over the course of her career, Twain has sold more than 100 million records worldwide, won five Grammy Awards and cemented her status as a country music icon.
However, Twain faced new obstacles even after reaching superstardom, including divorce and a battle with Lyme disease.
Twain also battled Lyme disease that affected her vocal cords and didn't release a new album for 15 years. (Dave J Hogan)

In 2003, she was diagnosed with Lyme disease, which affected her vocal cords and threatened her singing career. The ordeal contributed to a 15-year gap between studio albums before she returned with 2017's "Now," which debuted at No. 1 on the Billboard 200 chart.
In 2018, Twain underwent open-throat surgery and returned to touring. During her appearance on "CBS Mornings," she reflected on regaining her voice after her health struggles.

"Once I made a sound, it was just there," Twain recalled. "I feel lucky. I don't want to make it sound easy! It wasn't easy, it was a very long road, but I just feel very grateful and very lucky that I have it back."
"I have more, like, of a fry to my voice, you know, a little gravel," she continued. "I don't mind that. I've embraced it. It's now part of my sound."
Twain explained that she has adapted to the changes in her voice since resuming her career.
"I've taken a different approach to singing my older songs," she said. "In fact, I've found new placements in my voice that I enjoy, you know, that I didn't have before."

"I love to experiment. I think it's the same with any art form," Twain added. "You have to experiment a little bit to get just the right – whatever's satisfying you the most at that time, you know?"
Twain recently fulfilled a lifelong dream when she performed at Toronto's legendary venue Horseshoe Tavern. (Jeffrey Mayer/WireImage)
Twain recently fulfilled a longtime dream when she surprised fans with a performance at Toronto's legendary Horseshoe Tavern.

After taking the stage on Friday night, she told the crowd, "I grew up in Northern Ontario and the dream in my little bar bands at the time, all through my youth and my teens, even in my 20s, was to play the Horseshoe Tavern."
"But we weren’t recognized … we just weren’t established enough, so we never made the hire here," she continued. "So this is my first time in the Horseshoe Tavern."
LIKE WHAT YOU'RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE ENTERTAINMENT NEWS

"I guess I’ve finally made it after all these years," Twain added as the crowd cheered. "It was really a big deal to be able to play the Horseshoe Tavern. We all talked about that up North, ‘Oh, maybe someday we can play the Horseshoe Tavern.’ And now I’m playing here. I feel like it’s a very full-circle moment,"
Twain said her new album "Little Miss Twain" is inspired by her journey. (Getty Images)
"My home province, with all you beautiful people, in this historic bar. This is so historical. So it’s a privilege to be here, finally."
While speaking with "CBS Mornings," Twain explained how viewing her past struggles through a new lens had inspired her new album "Little Miss Twain."

"'Little Miss Twain' is me, now, looking back at my child's self and the journey that child went through, from starting out in those bars at 8 years old, right up to when I got my recording contract in Nashville," she said.

Though she acknowledged that it took decades to feel like she had"gotten it right," Twain said she is content with the timing.
"That's fine," she said. "I plan to live to be 200 anyway!"

title: Brad Paisley says Taylor Swift and Travis Kelce threw 'one of the least pretentious weddings' ever
summary: Brad Paisley says Taylor Swift and Travis Kelce's July 3 wedding was "one of the least pretentious" he'd ever attended despite hosting about 1,000 celebrity guests.
story: Fox News political analyst Gianno Caldwell and pundit Tiffany Smiley dissect the reported wedding of Taylor Swift and Travis Kelce on 'Fox News Saturday Night.'
Despite hosting roughly 1,000 guests, Taylor Swift and Travis Kelce kept their wedding refreshingly down-to-earth, according to one country music star.
Brad Paisley praised the couple's July 3 nuptials as refreshingly humble, calling the event of the decade "one of the least pretentious weddings" he'd ever attended.

"I took this personally when I got the invite, because in the invite, it said, ‘If you’re getting this, you mean a lot to us,’" Paisley told The Associated Press. "And it was really fun to watch the cat-and-mouse game of like, ‘We can tell you roughly where it’s gonna be. We’re not gonna say what building... And here’s the date, and if you’re in, we’ll tell you more.’ And I was like, I went to my wife, I said, ‘Want to go?’ She’s like, ‘Absolutely. We’ve gotta be there.’ So we did it. It was RSVP yes."
TAYLOR SWIFT AND TRAVIS KELCE'S WEDDING LEAKS SNOWBALL AS GUESTS REVEAL INSIDE DETAILS

Taylor Swift and Travis Kelce celebrated their July 3 wedding with roughly 1,000 guests, but country star Brad Paisley said it was "one of the least pretentious weddings" he has ever attended. (Getty Images)

title: 'Game of Thrones' star Lena Headey says outrage over infamous nude scene left her stunned
summary: Lena Headey reveals why she used a body double for Cersei's "Walk of Atonement" and reflects on the predatory power dynamics young actresses face.
story: Fox News Flash top entertainment and celebrity headlines are here.
More than 10 years after one of television's most talked-about scenes, Lena Headey set the record straight about a decision that sparked backlash far beyond Westeros.
Headey pulled back the curtain on the backlash that erupted after Cersei Lannister's infamous "Walk of Atonement" in "Game of Thrones," revealing she still found the outrage baffling.

"I was really shocked by the anger, by this idea that I’d duped the audience," Headey told The Telegraph. "But by that point everyone knew [the cast], it was insane simply going anywhere, and I was with 3,000 extras."
'OFF CAMPUS' STAR ELLA BRIGHT ADDRESSES AGE CONCERNS OVER INTIMATE SCENES IN PROVOCATIVE SERIES
Lena Headey reflected on the backlash she received after using a body double for Cersei Lannister's infamous "Walk of Atonement" scene in "Game of Thrones." (C Flanigan/Getty Images)

She explained that while acting is "a joy," the scale of filming the scene would have made it impossible for her to fully inhabit the emotional performance if she had also been worrying about being naked in front of thousands of people.
"I wouldn’t have been able to do the emotional part of the job," she told the outlet. "I’d have been in full-on defensive mode."

Looking back, Headey said she was in a very different position than many younger actresses entering the industry. Her experience on set gave her the confidence to set boundaries she doesn't believe everyone feels comfortable asserting.
GOLDIE HAWN SOUNDS THE ALARM ON CHILDHOOD CELEBRITY CULTURE: 'ALL I CAN SAY IS IT'S A NIGHTMARE'
Lena Headey and Nikolaj Coster-Waldau in a scene from season 7 of "Game of Thrones." The two played Cersei and Jaime Lannister in the series.  (Hbo/Kobal / Shutterstock)

"By that point, I’d been through the wringer," the actress said. "I could stand up for myself. I’m not saying those actresses couldn’t, but they were much younger and more vulnerable, and had far less experience of being in front of people and the camera and performing. Whereas I was of an age where I’d just tit about and diffuse anything uncomfortable with idiocy."
At the time, Headey told Entertainment Weekly some viewers believed she was "less of an actress" because she didn't perform the nudity herself.

"I've done nudity. I'm not averse to it," she explained in 2016. "But I know I'm a very emotional actor and I get really driven by that. In order to do my job, I allow myself to be really vulnerable. I don't know any other way to do my job. Things really affect me. And the thought of being naked for three days and trying to contain her in the way she would be I think I would feel very angry. I didn't want to be angry. I don't think Cersei would be angry. I did what I thought she would do, emotionally."
Lena Headey said filming Cersei Lannister's iconic "Game of Thrones" scene with thousands of extras made using a body double the right choice for her performance. (Kevin Winter/Getty Images)

Headey praised body double Rebecca Van Cleave for taking on the physically demanding role, acknowledging that appearing nude on camera was far from easy. She also said being a mother and an established public figure made filming the nude portions herself feel like more than she was willing to take on.
"I didn't phone it in," she noted of her performance. "I was actually there for three days with Rebecca."

Lena Headey portrayed the ruthless and power-hungry Queen Cersei Lannister throughout HBO's hit fantasy series "Game of Thrones," earning multiple Emmy nominations for the role. (Jason LaVeris/FilmMagic)
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR THE ENTERTAINMENT NEWSLETTER
For Headey, the controversy also reflected a much bigger issue she believes many actresses faced early in their careers.

"There was this rite of passage all young female actors had to go through, which usually involved snogging and falling in love, and having sex and showing your boobs," she told The Telegraph. "They’d call them the ingénue parts, to make it sound nicer."
The "300" actress admitted she rarely questioned those expectations when she was starting out because she was simply grateful to be working.

"But I just got on with it," she explained. "I didn’t go to drama school, so I would just arrive on a set and be, ‘Oh my God, I’ve got a job.’ And when it came to those moments, I don’t think I even questioned that I should be safe. Instead, I’d go home and cry, or think, ‘Oh, that felt weird and too familiar.’ Now I look back and feel, ‘Hmm, that was rough.’"
LIKE WHAT YOU'RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE ENTERTAINMENT NEWS

Lena Headey said her early experiences in Hollywood shaped the boundaries she later set as an established actress, reflecting on changing attitudes toward women in the entertainment industry. (Getty Images)
Those experiences ultimately changed the way Headey viewed power dynamics throughout the entertainment industry.

"The weird protection that we offer predatory men in the business because of the disproportionate power they wield, set against the need among vulnerable actresses to work to put food on the table to get the job – it makes me very angry. A job can be completely soured by one person who, for some reason, is allowed to get away with it."
She said the #MeToo movement exposed how widespread those experiences were and believes younger actresses today are far more willing to reject situations that make them uncomfortable.
"The attitude today is, ‘I’m not f---ing doing that,'" she emphasized.

title: Hayden Panettiere defends giving up custody of her daughter despite intense 'emotional pain'
summary: Hayden Panettiere reveals in her memoir why she gave full custody of daughter Kaya to Wladimir Klitschko while battling postpartum depression.
story: The "Sleepwalker" actress told Fox News Digital that she has learned to not be so hard on herself as she gets older in the industry.
Hayden Panettiere is opening up about what she calls the most painful decision she's ever made as a mother.

In her memoir, "This Is Me: A Reckoning," the "Nashville" alum opens up about why she gave full custody of her daughter, Kaya, to her ex-fiancé, Wladimir Klitschko. Panettiere reveals that her 11-year-old daughter has lived with her father since 2018.
"I just knew that if I wanted to... I knew how bad a place I was in," the actress told Fox News Digital. "I hid it from my daughter as much as I could."
HAYDEN PANETTIERE SAYS FILMING ‘NASHVILLE’ WAS LIKE LIVING THROUGH ADDICTION TWICE
Hayden Panettiere is opening up about the heartbreaking decision that led to daughter Kaya living with ex-fiancé Wladimir Klitschko since 2018. (Storm Santos)

"When I saw her in the environment over there (in Europe) and the support system that she had, I said to myself, 'If I fight, if I go to war about this, it's going to permanently damage my child. It's going to be incredibly public. She's got two very famous parents, and it's going to be ugly.'"

"I said, 'You know what? Let her grow up here,'" she said. "I will travel here as much as I can. I know she's safe. I know she's well taken care of — beyond well taken care of. She has an incredible life. And I also knew that there would be a day when she would come back to me."
"This Is Me: A Reckoning" by Hayden Panettiere is out now. (Grand Central Publishing)
"I tried to numb myself," the 36-year-old admitted. "It was very hard to wrap my mind around the pain, the emotional pain of that. But you keep putting one foot in front of the other somehow."
WATCH: HAYDEN PANETTIERE EXPLAINS THE MENTAL AND PHYSICAL CHALLENGES OF MAKING NEW THRILLER ‘SLEEPWALKER’
In the book, Panettiere wrote that not being under the same roof as Kaya has been "the most gut-wrenching experience of my life."

"... I grieve that I'm not the mother I thought I'd be and definitely not the mother I want to be (trust me, no one should ever have to raise a child on FaceTime), and although I miss Kaya so much, my heart aches, I know how blessed I am to be her mom."
Hayden Panettiere told Fox News Digital she hopes sharing her story will help mothers battling postpartum depression feel less alone. (Bernd Thissen/Picture Alliance via Getty Images)
Panettiere reflected on filming "Nashville" while navigating a difficult pregnancy, which was ultimately written into her character Juliette Barnes' storyline.
On the set of "Nashville," art imitated life for Hayden Panettiere in ways she never expected. (Mark Levine/Disney General Entertainment Content via Getty Images)

Panettiere's pregnancy was marked by a series of frightening health scares. She described how doctors spotted concerning abnormalities during prenatal scans and warned that Kaya might have microcephaly. The actress sought solace in Hawaii, a place she has long considered a refuge.
While she was there, Klitschko shared a Ukrainian tradition for good luck, urging her to kneel before a tree, hold onto it and "thank God for everything He has given you and pray for what you need."
Hayden Panettiere is seen here in Hawaii shortly before her daughter was born. (Courtesy of Hayden Panettiere)

Weeks later, Panettiere endured a life-threatening delivery. During her C-section, doctors called a "code crimson" after her blood wouldn't clot and her uterus became infected. She underwent three hours of emergency surgery.
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR THE ENTERTAINMENT NEWSLETTER
Hayden Panettiere is seen with her growing baby bump. She gave birth on Dec. 9, 2014. (Courtesy of Hayden Panettiere)
"I almost passed away while having my daughter," Panettiere told Fox News Digital. "I had seven blood transfusions. I didn't know if I was going to make it."
During her recovery, Panettiere struggled to bond with her daughter.
Hayden Panettiere and Wladimir Klitschko met at a party for a mutual friend in 2008. (Courtesy of Hayden Panettiere)

"You hear these stories from your friends about their experiences, and they're so positive," she said. "They also tell you about 'the baby blues.' At first, I thought, 'I just have the baby blues.' But it just kept going and going, deeper and deeper, worse and worse. And the doctors wouldn't even diagnose me with anything. My way of trying to cope with it was drinking because of the anxiety and the inability to sleep."
In her new memoir, Hayden Panettiere detailed the struggles she endured with postpartum depression. (Storm Santos)

"You are just discontent and unhappy all the time," Panettiere said. "You just feel like it's really dark. It doesn't make rational sense. It's not logical. And yet, you're trying to make sense of it. But when it's going on for 10 months afterward, you're like, there's something seriously wrong."

In the memoir, Panettiere recalled enduring "long days of nothingness stretching before me" as anxiety took over, becoming "the hulking monster that sits in your chest and erases your confidence and motivation." Despite having "everything I've ever wanted," she remained deeply "unhappy."
Wladimir Klitschko and Hayden Panettiere attend the Giorgio Armani show during Milan Menswear Fashion Week Spring/Summer 2014 on June 25, 2013, in Milan, Italy. (Venturelli/WireImage)
She self-medicated with alcohol. The actress entered treatment for the first time when Kaya was 4 months old after realizing her drinking had spiraled out of control.
LIKE WHAT YOU’RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE ENTERTAINMENT NEWS

When Kaya was 4 months old, Hayden Panettiere sought treatment and was diagnosed with postpartum depression. She says the medications she was prescribed left her feeling numb and disconnected. (Storm Santos)
"When you wake up in the morning and the first thing you're thinking about is having a drink, it's a problem," Panettiere said.
Panettiere realized she needed treatment.
Hayden Panettiere and Wladimir Klitschko ended their relationship for good in 2018. (Jemal Countess/Getty Images)

"I just knew that I had to get help, do it for myself. I knew I was no good in the condition that I was in. I did everything that I could, and I came out sober, but I was still struggling with postpartum. But I was the one who asked to go to treatment."
"I walked into rehab addicted to one substance, and I walked out, completely dependent on something else," Hayden Panettiere wrote in her memoir. (Martin Rose/Bongarts/Getty Images)
Panettiere said she reached a breaking point and realized she needed professional help after alcohol became her way of coping with persistent postpartum depression following childbirth.

"I talked to my daughter's father about it, and I was like, 'I need help, professional help. I need somebody to fix me because this depression for the rest of my... is it ever going to go away? Is this the new normal? Am I going to have to just understand that I'm going to always be depressed for the rest of my life?' So when I went to treatment, it was me going, 'I'm at my breaking point. I need intervention. I need professionals. I need somebody to guide me through this.'"
Hayden Panettiere began her first regular acting role at age 4 in "One Life to Live." (Ron Galella/Getty Images; Jon Kopaloff/Getty Images)

In the book, Panettiere wrote that in 2015, the anxiety "crept back in, then overtook me," buzzing "like a fluorescent light, keeping me reactive, on edge and full of dread." She became reliant on prescription medication to help her cope.
CLICK HERE TO GET THE FOX NEWS APP
Hayden Panettiere starred in the television series "Nashville" for six seasons from 2012 to 2018. (Courtesy of Hayden Panettiere)

As Panettiere continued battling addiction and mental health challenges, her relationship with Klitschko unraveled. In 2018, he presented her with papers seeking full custody of Kaya, telling her, "I want full custody. I worry about Kaya when she's with you."

Panettiere defended herself, insisting their daughter was always surrounded by loving caregivers and that she had "never been drunk and alone with Kaya" while she was in her care. Even so, she ultimately chose not to contest the custody arrangement, writing that she believed it was the best decision for Kaya while she worked to rebuild her life.
Panettiere wrote that much of her character's story in season four of "Nashville" was based on her own personal struggles. (Dimitrios Kambouris/Getty Images)
"I was mortified when I saw stories like 'Hayden Panettiere gave up her daughter,'" she said.
Hayden Panettiere is pushing back against claims she "gave up" her daughter. (Storm Santos)

"I was heartbroken. It's not like I live for other people's opinions of me, but I'm also a human being. Everyone wants to be understood. And I had to tell myself every day that she's in an amazing environment. She's learning different languages. She's passionate about horseback riding. She has friends, she has a great support system."
"I felt like I made the right call," she reflected. "I've seen who she is and she's an incredible human being. Something must have gone right."
Panettiere recalled realizing she needed to seek help for her addiction when she found herself searching for alcohol at 6 a.m. (Raymond Hall/GC Images)
Panettiere wrote that she has an "incredibly strong" bond with Kaya.
HAYDEN PANETTIERE SAYS GROWING UP IN HOLLYWOOD MADE HER ‘VERY PROTECTIVE’ OF KIDS ON SET
Hayden Panettiere describes her relationship with ex-fiancé Wladimir Klitschko today as "kind." (Luca Teuchmann/Getty Images)

"I travel a lot to Europe, and I spend a lot of time on FaceTime with her," she explained. "And Wlad and I have a good relationship. We made a promise to each other that we would never say a bad word about each other to our child. That was something that I grew up with. And we've stuck to that."

"She's 11 now, so time is flying," Panettiere said. "I feel like she's becoming more and more curious about me, my life and who I am. We're so similar. She is me. I understand her in a way that nobody else can."
Hayden Panettiere discusses "Nashville" with the Build Series at AOL HQ on Jan. 5, 2017, in New York City. (Roy Rochlin/FilmMagic)
Today, Panettiere said she's doing "great" and hopes sharing her story will encourage other mothers suffering in silence to seek help.
Hayden Panettiere told Fox News Digital she's doing "great" and has a close bond with her daughter Kaya. (Michael Buckner/Variety via Getty Images)

"I feel connected to myself," she said. "I feel like I'm taking good care of myself, checking in with myself. And I have a laundry list of things I would love to accomplish and create. I feel more connected with myself than I ever have before."
Stephanie Nolasco is an Entertainment Reporter for Fox News Digital.

title: Jennifer Lopez reveals what makes a man 'sexy' to her
summary: Jennifer Lopez revealed what she finds sexiest in a man during her Dolce & Gabbana performance in Sicily, and it has nothing to do with money.
story: Fox News Flash top entertainment and celebrity headlines are here.
Jennifer Lopez revealed what she finds sexiest in a man.
The singer and actress shared her thoughts on it during her performance at the Dolce & Gabbana show in Taormina, Sicily, on Thursday.
"But you know what really makes a man attractive? It’s not the watch. It’s not the car. It’s not the private jet. It really isn’t, although that’s nice," the 56-year-old star began.
"It’s nice. It’s seeing them make the bed in the morning or wash the dishes for you when you’re tired at night. That’s what’s sexy. Now that’s what I call sexy," she continued.
TIM ALLEN REVEALS THE ONE THING THAT HAS SAVED HIS NEARLY 20-YEAR MARRIAGE TO JANE HAJDUK
Jennifer Lopez revealed what she finds sexiest in a man. (John Nacion/WireImage)
"Cause ladies, you know, we do all the things. We do all the things," Lopez concluded.
According to People magazine, the audience laughed and applauded her.
JENNIFER LOPEZ TAKES BLAME FOR BEN AFFLECK DIVORCE, SAYS SHE NEEDED TO 'FIGURE' HERSELF OUT AFTER SPLIT
Lopez performed a number of her songs, including "Love Don’t Cost a Thing," "Waiting For Tonight," "Let’s Get Loud," "Ain’t Your Mama" and "Save Me Tonight."
The mother of two wore a sparkling bodysuit for her performance.
Prior to speaking about what she finds sexiest in men, Lopez had a playful exchange with one of her backup dancers, per People.
J-Lo also had a playful exchange with her backup dancer. (Ricardo Rubio/Europa Press via Getty Images)
JENNIFER ANISTON SUPPORTS JUSTIN THEROUX BABY NEWS AS A-LISTERS TURN BREAK-UPS INTO FRIENDSHIPS
"Fix my hair OK. Fix my hair. But the rest of you, get out of here. You’re broke. I don’t need you. I don’t need your money. I don’t need your gifts. That’s right," she told him.

She then added: "You know, people look at me, they look at me for years, and they think I’m expensive. You see my sparkly cup. And I am, I am expensive. You see my sparkly cup. And I am, I am expensive," she said with a laugh.
"I am, but I have my own money. Ladies, am I right? We don’t need anybody to buy us anything. We don’t. We want them to, sometimes that’s nice."
Recently, Lopez opened up about why her most recent divorce ended up being "the best thing" for her.
During an interview on SiriusXM's "The Howard Stern Show," the star discussed her 2024 divorce from Ben Affleck, detailing what she learned from the split.

"When I got divorced this last time, it was the best thing that ever happened to me," she explained. "Because it really made me journey into — I mean, I had a religious coach. I had a therapist, a couple's therapist, an individual therapist. I had a coach to understand addiction. I had everything. I was like, 'I'm gonna f---in' figure this s--- out if it kills me.'"
The "Hustlers" star has been married four times, including to Marc Anthony from 2004 to 2014, and to Affleck from 2022 to 2024.

"What I learned, it's not that I'm not lovable — it's that they're not capable... They don't have it in them," she explained, adding, "And they gave me what they had. They gave me all of it, every time. All the rings, all the things I could ever want. The houses, the rings, the marriage. All of it. But.…"
J-Lo performed in Italy at the Dolce & Gabbana show. (Mariano Regidor)
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
After working through her divorce, Lopez noted she is "able to sit here in a much more self-assured, self-aware way" and reflect on everything that has happened in her life.

"Whether my mother, my father, in my own life, how I learned to love, how I felt neglected — all the things that are in your head as a person — and know who I am and just really appreciate that person," she said. "[I] feel really comfortable and good in being myself, all the good parts and all the kind of complicated things."

title: 'Resurrection of the Christ' writer reveals Mel Gibson's dark spiritual warning about 'Passion' follow-up
summary: Randall Wallace reveals Mel Gibson warned him that "Satan's going to come after you" before they began writing "The Resurrection of the Christ."
story: Fox News contributor Raymond Arroyo calls out the ultimate threat to democracy in Los Angeles and dissects a musical glorifying accused United Healthcare CEO killer Luigi Mangione on The Ingraham Angle.
Mel Gibson's longtime collaborator Randall Wallace revealed the dark spiritual warning that the two-time Oscar winner gave him before they began writing the follow-up to "The Passion of the Christ."

The 76-year-old screenwriter, who previously teamed up with the 70-year-old director and actor for 1995's "Braveheart," 2002's "We Were Soldiers" and 2016's "Hacksaw Ridge," co-wrote the screenplay for "The Resurrection of the Christ" with Gibson and his brother Donal Gibson.

During a recent appearance on Raymond Arroyo's podcast "Arroyo Grande," Wallace recalled how he urged Gibson to tell the Resurrection story following the massive success of "The Passion of the Christ."
MEL GIBSON'S 'RESURRECTION OF THE CHRIST' REVEALS FIRST PHOTOS AFTER LONG-AWAITED PASSION FOLLOW-UP
"Mel didn't approach me. I approached him, actually," Wallace said of how they began working together on "The Resurrection of the Christ."

Mel Gibson's longtime collaborator revealed the stark warning that the director gave him before they began co-writing "The Resurrection of the Christ." (Domenico Cippitelli/NurPhoto via Getty Images; Elise Lockwood for Lionsgate)

"This is not to say that over the years, he hadn't thought many times about the Resurrection," Wallace continued. "In fact, in the original ‘The Passion of the Christ,’ the original cut didn't have the resurrection scene. He was getting feedback from people saying, 'We really want to see that.'"
Wallace said Gibson ultimately decided to add the brief Resurrection scene that serves as "The Passion of the Christ's" closing epilogue.
In the sequence, Jesus is seen rising, leaving the tomb, and revealing the wounds in his hands before the movie ends.
Randall Wallace co-wrote the follow-up to the 2004 mega-hit with Gibson and the director's brother Donal Gibson. (Mary Evans/Ronald Grant/Everett Collection)
Wallace told Arroyo that he proposed developing a feature-length film depicting the Resurrection while he and Gibson were on a promotional tour for "Hacksaw Ridge" in 2016.

"Having studied the Resurrection and being so consumed by it, I thought about it many times," Wallace recalled. "I didn't have anything to do with ‘The Passion of the Christ.’ When we were promoting ‘Hacksaw Ridge,’ we were sitting there talking about our lives, and I said, ‘Look, you know, the story that you really need to tell is the Resurrection.’"
Wallace went on to recount Gibson's reaction to his suggestion, remembering that the director believed the project could invite spiritual warfare.
Wallace recalled that Gibson warned him, "Satan's going to come after you." (Tommaso Boddi/Getty Images)

"There was this long pause, and he said something profoundly beautiful. He said, 'If we do this, it can't be for the money, and it can't be to get back at people that have hated us or wronged us or been unhappy with us,'" Wallace recalled. "And I said, ‘Amen to that.’"
"Then he said, 'You know, Satan's going to come after you,'" Wallace continued.
"I said, 'Well, you know, Satan doesn't really care about Baptists.' It's really good when Satan can get a Catholic. We're a dime a dozen," he said as Arroyo laughed.
"And of course, I was being facetious, but I was also thinking…" Wallace continued.
"What if he's right?" Arroyo interjected.
"Well, yeah," Wallace admitted.
"That's what I would be thinking," Arroyo said.
"We had a beautiful conversation about grace," Wallace recalled.
Wallace said he pitched Gibson on the follow-up when they were promoting 2016's "Hacksaw Ridge." (Mike Marsland/Mike Marsland/WireImage via Getty Images)
Wallace told Arroyo that conversation with Gibson marked the beginning of their collaboration on "The Resurrection of the Christ."

"I knew he had written ‘The Passion,’ was very much deeply involved in the writing of it. And I said, 'Look, let's partner up. I'll write a draft, give it to you, then we'll start tearing it up, go through it. You do your thing, I'll do mine. We'll work together, we'll work apart.' So we started that way," Wallace remembered.
Gibson has previously said he, Wallace and Donal spent roughly six to eight years writing and refining the screenplay for "The Resurrection of the Christ," which will be split into two parts.
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR THE ENTERTAINMENT NEWSLETTER

In May, Gibson announced that production on the follow-up had been completed. "The Resurrection of the Christ: Part One" will be released May 6, 2027, on Ascension Day, the Christian holiday marking Jesus Christ’s ascent into heaven 40 days after Easter Sunday. "The Resurrection of the Christ: Part Two" is scheduled to debut May 25, 2028, over Memorial Day weekend.
Jaakko Ohtonen is starring as Jesus in "The Resurrection of the Christ: Part One." (Elise Lockwood for Lionsgate)
In a press release, Gibson shared that the story was brought to the screen "exactly as I envisioned it."
"I’m deeply grateful to my incredibly talented cast and crew for pouring their hearts into this production. Together, we created something powerful," Gibson said.

"This film represents a major part of my life’s work, and it has demanded everything of me as a filmmaker and as an artist. This is far more than a film to me. It’s a mission I’ve carried for over 20 years to tell what I believe is the most important story in human history," he added.
LIKE WHAT YOU'RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE ENTERTAINMENT NEWS

"The Passion of the Christ," which premiered in February 2004, depicted the final 12 hours of Jesus’ life leading up to the crucifixion. Its graphic violence and subject matter made it one of that year's most controversial movies.
The film was a smash hit, grossing more than $610 million worldwide on a reported $30 million budget. It also earned Academy Award nominations for its makeup, score and cinematography.
"The Passion of the Christ" starred Jim Caviezel as Jesus of Nazareth. (Lionsgate/Fathom Entertainment)
While speaking with Arroyo, Wallace teased what audiences can expect from the long-awaited follow-up.
"His unique vision of the spiritual realm is really special," Wallace said of Gibson.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

"The interesting thing is that, while in some ways — the ultimate movie — I want to keep it all secret about what's going to happen," he continued. "But the ultimate movie, in some ways, will have elements that people have never seen before."

"In fact, in many ways, it'll be stuff nobody's ever seen," Wallace added. "And yet I believe it'll be, in a certain way, the most orthodox telling. It'll be the most consistent telling of the overall belief, the awe and the mystery that Christians experience when they experience the Resurrection."
Ashley Hume is an entertainment journalist for Fox News Digital and Fox Business who covers breaking news, celebrity culture, major industry events and the business of entertainment.

title: Gisele Bündchen stuns in white bikini as she shares rare glimpse of baby son during family getaway in Tahiti
summary: Gisele Bündchen shared rare photos of her baby son with Joaquim Valente during a fun-filled Tahiti family vacation with all three of her children.
story: Fox News Flash top entertainment and celebrity headlines are here.
Gisele Bündchen showed off her summer style as she shared rare photos of herself with her one-year-old son while enjoying a family vacation in Tahiti.

On Saturday, the 45-year-old supermodel posted a carousel of snaps that included images of her youngest child, her husband Joaquim Valente and her older children Benjamin Rein, 16, and Vivian Lake, 13, whom she shares with her ex-husband Tom Brady, 48.
Bündchen and Valente married in 2025, months after welcoming their son, whose name they have not publicly revealed.
SHAKIRA SOAKS UP THE MIAMI SUN AS BIKINI-CLAD NINA DOBREV, KIM KARDASHIAN SHOWCASE SUMMER GETAWAYS
In the first photo, Bündchen donned a white bikini and a straw hat as she stood in the ocean hand in hand with her baby son, who wore matching white swim trunks.
Gisele Bündchen stunned in a white bikini as she shared rare photos of her one-year-old son while on a family vacation in Tahiti.  (Gisele Bundchen Instagram)

The former Victoria's Secret Angel uploaded a selfie in which she was seen in a pink sleeveless knit dress that she paired with delicate gold necklaces and a white lei. Bündchen also sported a crown made of tropical flowers as she smiled at the camera.
In another photo, Bündchen wore the same ensemble while dancing with her baby son and Valente to live music played by Tahitian performers.

Valente was seen enjoying some quality time with their child in one snap that Bündchen shared. The jiu-jitsu instructor wore snorkeling goggles on his head and black swim trunks as he stood in the ocean while holding up their son as what appeared to be a stingray swam by in the water below them.
Bündchen was seen wearing a floral crown in one selfie. (Gisele Bundchen Instagram)

Bündchen also captured sweet moments that her children shared during the family trip. In one photo, Benjamin was seen holding his younger half-sibling while on a boat as they looked down at the waves.

Vivian was also seen on the boat while tenderly embracing her baby brother in another snap. Bündchen also included a photo of Vivian wrapping her arm around her older brother as the two enjoyed a scenic view from on top of a cliff.
In other images, the family was seen bike riding, snorkeling, doing headstands in the ocean, enjoying tropical scenery, eating fresh fruit and stargazing.

title: CDC reveals massive behind-the-scenes public health operation that kept FIFA World Cup fans safe
summary: The CDC operated behind the scenes during the FIFA World Cup, deploying disease surveillance, wastewater monitoring and real-time data dashboards.
story: Andrew Giuliani outlines the significant economic and security preparations for the 2026 FIFA World Cup. He reveals 78 matches will occur across 11 cities, projecting a $30.5 billion boost to the American economy.

FIRST ON FOX: The World Cup tested not only the players on the pitch, but the Trump administration's large public health operation to safeguard the public as fans from all over the world moved across the United States.

Amid the fandom, as 11 American cities hosted 39 teams and 78 matches, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) operated largely behind the scenes to detect emerging threats and to respond to public health emergencies.
"Readiness is not only measured by how we respond to emergencies, but by the work we do every day to prevent them," acting CDC Director Dr. Jay Bhattacharya said in a statement to Fox News Digital.
"The FIFA World Cup demonstrated the strength of CDC’s partnerships, preparedness and commitment to protecting the health of every community we serve."
CONGO TEAM MUST ISOLATE TO ENTER UNITED STATES FOR WORLD CUP AMID EBOLA OUTBREAK

Fans gather before the FIFA World Cup 2026 final match between Spain and Argentina at New Jersey Stadium, also known as MetLife Stadium, in East Rutherford, N.J., July 19, 2026. The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention tracked public health threats behind the scenes during the tournament. (Anadolu via Getty Images)
In total, the FIFA World Cup hosted 48 teams across 16 cities in the U.S., Canada and Mexico, with more than 5 million tickets sold.

An estimated 6.5 million fans from around the world converged in the three host countries, bringing their passion, enthusiasm and, possibly, germs. Overlapping with Independence Day celebrations, large gatherings were common, as well as the backdrop of concurrent international disease activity, including the Ebola and Hantavirus outbreaks.
Infectious disease can easily spread in large crowds, and experts were already looking at wastewater, a possible uptick in hospital visits and social media for any signs of a potential outbreak.
Diseases like measles are always a top concern. As of July 16, there were 2,260 confirmed measles cases in the U.S., according to the CDC.
"The matches drew the world's attention. The work that kept them healthy did not — and that was the point," the CDC said in a news release Sunday.
FBI BOSS KASH PATEL DETAILS HOW AGENCY AND PARTNERS SECURED RECORD-SHATTERING FIFA WORLD CUP
MetLife Stadium in East Rutherford, N.J., hosted games during the 2026 World Cup. (Getty Images)

The CDC's effort included a World Cup data dashboard that provided health departments with real-time data on disease trends across multiple cities as fans and teams traveled throughout the tournament, as well as around-the-clock health operations at U.S. ports of entry in coordination with U.S. Customs and Border Protection to monitor international passengers.
The agency also deployed its experts to strengthen disease surveillance, laboratory capacity, wastewater surveillance and preparedness planning in host cities.

In all, the agency coordinated across a broad network, including multiple CDC divisions, the Department of Health and Human Services (HHS), the Administration for Strategic Preparedness and Response (ASPR) and the White House FIFA World Cup Task Force.
WHITE HOUSE ADDRESSES GROWING PARASITE OUTBREAK AFTER MORE THAN 400 AMERICANS SICKENED

In March, the CDC released guidance providing health officials with a framework for preparing for a broad range of threats, including biological, chemical, radiologic/nuclear, environmental and mass casualty incidents.
The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) headquarters in Atlanta. (AP Photo/Jeff Amy, File)
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
The guidance encouraged every jurisdiction to approach the tournament through a risk-based lens, recognizing that travel between venues connects communities far beyond the host cities.

The tournament is over, but the work is not. The same preparedness, surveillance and partnerships that supported the World Cup are part of CDC's readiness and response mission every day of the year, continuing through the close of the activation on July 31 and well beyond.

title: Experts reveal how to avoid deadly Legionnaires' disease as NYC outbreak kills 5
summary: The New York City Legionnaires' disease outbreak has killed five and sickened 82, but doctors say key prevention steps can reduce exposure risk.
story: NYC health officials warn residents of a Legionnaires' disease outbreak with 23 confirmed cases. Dr. Stephanie Widmer explains the bacterial pneumonia, its symptoms like cough and fever and its curability.

As New York City continues to investigate an outbreak of Legionnaires' disease that has claimed multiple lives and sickened dozens of people, doctors say there are ways people can reduce the risk of exposure.

As of July 21, there have been five deaths and 82 diagnoses linked to the Upper East Side outbreak, according to the New York City Department of Health and Mental Hygiene. Eight patients remain hospitalized.
Health officials said no new cases had been reported in the previous six days, suggesting the source of exposure has likely been eliminated, although the investigation remains ongoing.
NYC LEGIONNAIRES' DISEASE OUTBREAK KILLS FOURTH VICTIM; 76 CASES REPORTED
Legionnaires’ disease is a serious type of pneumonia that is typically spread by tiny water droplets containing Legionella bacteria, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention.

As New York City continues to investigate an outbreak of Legionnaires' disease that has claimed multiple lives and sickened dozens of people, doctors say there are ways people can reduce the risk of exposure. (iStock)
Sources of exposure

Common sources of infection include contaminated building water systems, such as cooling towers (large structures that remove heat from water used in building cooling systems), hot tubs or plumbing. Cases have also been reported on cruise ships and in spas. It is not generally spread from person to person, according to the CDC.

"We get infected when it gets aerosolized in the water droplets, usually, and we breathe those droplets in," Dr. Dana Mordue, associate professor of pathology, microbiology and immunology at New York Medical College, told Fox News Digital.
NYC HEALTH OFFICIALS WARN CENTRAL PARK VISITORS AFTER LEGIONNAIRES’ OUTBREAK GROWS ON UPPER EAST SIDE

"You can also get infected if you have water that's been contaminated, and you aspirate it and swallow it into your lungs, but most often you get it from air droplets that are contaminated from various types of water sources."
Legionnaires’ disease is a serious type of pneumonia that is typically spread by tiny water droplets containing Legionella bacteria. (iStock)

Although it is possible to contract Legionnaires’ in the home, outbreaks are almost always linked to exposure to water droplets coming from a water system in a "commercial-type building," according to Mordue.

"The good news is you usually don't get it from the types of cooling systems that we have in our cars or our homes. But if you don't clean your humidifiers, technically any water source can get contaminated with Legionella."
Symptoms and treatment

The most widespread symptoms of Legionnaires' disease include cough, shortness of breath, fever, muscle aches and headaches, according to the CDC. Some people may also experience diarrhea, nausea and confusion.
Symptoms typically begin two to 14 days after exposure to the bacteria, although they can appear later. The illness often requires treatment with antibiotics.
The most widespread symptoms of Legionnaires' disease include cough, shortness of breath, fever, muscle aches and headaches, according to the CDC.  (iStock)
"The mortality rate is not particularly high for this disease if you are immune-competent and young and healthy," said Mordue.
Risk is higher for older adults, smokers and people with compromised immune systems, "a lot of the same risk factors you might see for COVID," the doctor noted.
Ways to prevent spread
The CDC shares the following measures to prevent the spread of Legionnaires’ disease.

Maintain building water systems. Comprehensive water management programs can prevent Legionella bacteria from growing in cooling towers, plumbing systems, hot tubs and other building water systems. The CDC estimates that nearly nine in 10 outbreaks could have been prevented with more effective water management.Clean and disinfect cooling towers. These structures should be routinely cleaned, monitored and disinfected to control bacteria growth, health officials recommend.Prevent stagnant water. Maintaining proper water flow and flushing any pipes that are infrequently used can help prevent Legionella from multiplying.Maintain proper water temperature and disinfectant levels. As Legionella is known to grow best in warm water (about 77°F to 113°F), maintaining appropriate temperatures and adequate disinfectant levels helps limit bacterial growth, the CDC says.

Maintain building water systems. Comprehensive water management programs can prevent Legionella bacteria from growing in cooling towers, plumbing systems, hot tubs and other building water systems. The CDC estimates that nearly nine in 10 outbreaks could have been prevented with more effective water management.
Clean and disinfect cooling towers. These structures should be routinely cleaned, monitored and disinfected to control bacteria growth, health officials recommend.
Prevent stagnant water. Maintaining proper water flow and flushing any pipes that are infrequently used can help prevent Legionella from multiplying.

Maintain proper water temperature and disinfectant levels. As Legionella is known to grow best in warm water (about 77°F to 113°F), maintaining appropriate temperatures and adequate disinfectant levels helps limit bacterial growth, the CDC says.

For anyone who may have been exposed and developed symptoms, it is important to seek immediate medical care, doctors say. Early diagnosis and antibiotic treatment can reduce the risk of severe illness.
"If you have certain risk factors, particularly advanced age, get help as quickly as you can," Mordue advised.

title: Pancreatic cancer vaccine shows promise in first human trial, preventing disease in high-risk patients
summary: A Johns Hopkins pancreatic cancer vaccine triggered immune responses in 90% of high-risk participants, with some cysts shrinking after vaccination.
story: Fox News senior correspondent Jonathan Serrie reports on doctors seeing results from Daraxonrasib, a new drug targeting pancreatic cancer, on ‘Special Report.’
A new vaccine for the prevention of pancreatic cancer has shown promise in an early study at Johns Hopkins School of Medicine in Baltimore, Maryland.
A phase 1 trial published in Cancer Discovery, a journal of the American Association for Cancer Research, tested an experimental vaccine called mKRAS-VAX in 20 people, according to a press release.

Participants had an inherited risk of pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC), the most common and aggressive form of pancreatic cancer, along with an abnormality detected in imaging, typically a pancreatic cyst. These individuals had not been diagnosed with pancreatic cancer.
NEW PANCREATIC CANCER PILL NEARLY DOUBLES SURVIVAL TIME IN BREAKTHROUGH TRIAL
Four injections were administered to participants during weeks one, three and five, along with a booster at week 13.
The vaccine targeted six common mutations of KRAS. Changes in this gene drive more than 90% of PDACs.
The vaccine targeted six common mutations of KRAS. Changes in this gene drive more than 90% of PDACs. (iStock)

The vaccine triggered a mutant KRAS-targeted immune response in 18 of the 20 participants (90%). On average, immune activity increased about 18-fold, although responses varied. Half of participants responded to all six KRAS mutations included in the vaccine.
Researchers also found the vaccine generated two types of T cells — one to attack abnormal cells and another to provide longer-term immune memory.
TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ
The vaccine appeared to be safe, with participants experiencing only injection-site reactions and temporary flu-like symptoms.

While the phase 1 trial was designed primarily to evaluate safety rather than effectiveness, after about 16.5 months of follow-up, no participants had developed pancreatic cancer. At the same time, 37.5% of vaccinated participants experienced shrinkage or disappearance of the pancreatic cysts that had put them at increased risk for the disease.
Some pancreatic cancer cysts shrank or disappeared in vaccinated individuals, according to a press release. (iStock)

Study co-author Neeha Zaidi, MD, associate professor of oncology at the Sidney Kimmel Comprehensive Cancer Center at Johns Hopkins University, commented that the long-lasting response of this vaccine is "particularly noteworthy when assessing for possible interception of cancer, which requires long-lasting immunity."

"In addition, the vaccine was safe and well-tolerated, supporting its use in larger cancer interception studies," she said in the press release. "Overall, this study represents the first proof of concept for the use of vaccines for interception of pancreatic cancer in human patients."
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER

Co-author Michael G. Goggins, MD, professor of pathology, medicine and oncology and the Sol Goldman Professor of Pancreatic Cancer Research at Johns Hopkins University School of Medicine, also commented on the findings.
CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES

"We observed evidence of stability or regression of the pancreatic cysts in association with the induction and durability of KRAS-specific T-cell responses," he said in the release. "However, larger studies are needed to demonstrate that this effect was in fact due to the vaccine."
The authors noted the study was limited by its small sample size and because it was not designed to determine clinical efficacy.
Prevention and interception "save lives and reduce the morbidity associated with cancer development and progression," a co-author says. (iStock)

Fellow senior author Elizabeth Jaffee, MD, deputy director of the Sidney Kimmel Comprehensive Cancer Center at Johns Hopkins, commented that prevention and interception "save lives and reduce the morbidity associated with cancer development and progression."
"This is especially important for cancers whose early-onset frequency is increasing and for which we do not have effective methods for early detection," she added in the release.

Jaffee noted that this research highlights the need for more funding to support developing strategies for preventing cancer in high-risk individuals.
"More studies are needed to find the best vaccine approaches, the best targets and the ideal timing for vaccination," she said.
Angelica Stabile is a lifestyle reporter for Fox News Digital.

title: Michelin-star chef reveals what's replacing hospital food Americans love to hate
summary: Chef Geoffrey Zakarian reveals how he overhauled Tampa General Hospital's menu on a budget while eliminating seed oils and sugar and improving patient health.
story: After three years of rethinking hospital meals, Michelin star chef Geoffrey Zakarian is swapping boxed shakes, seed oils and sugar for fresh comfort food, smoothies and protein-rich dishes built around the idea that food can help with healing.
"Hospital food" has long been synonymous with packaged, ultraprocessed meals — despite the fact that hospitals are meant to promote healing.

In an exclusive interview with Fox News Digital at the Great American State Fair in Washington, D.C., Michelin-star chef Geoffrey Zakarian shared his initiative to improve what is served in U.S. hospitals, following the concept that "food is medicine."
For the last three years, Zakarian said he’s been working on changing hospital food — most notably at Tampa General, which is a $4 billion nonprofit, 1,000-bed public hospital.
RFK HAILS FIRST US HOSPITAL TO PROMISE HEALTHIER MEALS: 'WE HAVE A TEMPLATE'

On Thursday, July 16, Tampa General Hospital CEO John Couris signed the "Make Hospital Food Healthier" pledge during a news conference attended by Health and Human Services (HHS) Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr., U.S. Department of Agriculture (USDA) Secretary Brooke Rollins and Zakarian.
Michelin-star chef Geoffrey Zakarian sat down with Fox News Digital at the Great American State Fair in Washington, D.C., on July 6, 2026. (Angelica Stabile/Fox News Digital)
The pledge commits the hospital to serving more nutritious, minimally processed meals to patients, building on Zakarian's menu overhaul.
"We’ve changed the entire menu," the celebrity chef told Fox News Digital. "We've taken all seed oils out, sugar, maltodextrin. Anything bad in a box is gone. Anything good is brought in."
CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES

"We're serving mac and cheese. We're serving hanger steak and fries. We're serving chicken with couscous. We do all our protein shakes. No protein shakes in the box anymore. We do fruit shakes, smoothies, fresh sorbet," the chef listed. "So, you're eating like your grandmother's cooking for you."
CMS Administrator Dr. Mehmet Oz has also supported Zakarian in this mission, telling Fox News Digital that the chef has "revolutionized our thinking" around hospital food.

Michelin-star chef Geoffrey Zakarian and CMS Administrator Dr. Oz spoke with Fox News Digital at the Great American State Fair in Washington, D.C., on July 6, 2026. (Angelica Stabile/Fox News Digital)

"How do we get the hospitals to do what [Zakarian] has been doing the frontier work on, get them to actually embrace food as part of the healing process?" he questioned. "Because most patients, and most doctors, know that the food in the hospital is not going to make you better."
Oz noted that while hospital food may provide some nutrients, it is generally not seen as contributing meaningfully to patients' recovery.
TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ
The biggest challenge to getting better food into hospital systems has been cost, Zakarian pointed out.
While "everything is fractionalized," what’s left over after paying for supplies is put toward food, which generally "ain’t much," he said.
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER

"It's, like, $3.50 a person per plate, which is an extraordinarily small amount," the chef said. "You go to McDonald's, and you spend 12 bucks for a happy meal, and we give you $3.50 in a hospital. So that's an unhappy meal as far as I'm concerned."
Instead of charging hospitals for each plate served, Zakarian's approach relies on a flat annual fee, saving money through a smaller, higher-quality menu.
Tampa General Hospital (not pictured) worked with a chef to revamp its menu and make it more nutritious. (iStock)
"Yummy food, not just food to fill people up," he said. "Nutritious food, bioavailable food, food that's satiating."
"I'm cooking like I would cook in a restaurant. I'm cooking like my mother cooked for me. There's no difference."

The chef continued, "When you're lying in bed in a hospital gown, you feel alone, you feel exposed, you feel sick … When you have a fresh protein shake or a fresh healthy smoothie, or you can order steak frites ... that [makes] your day."
Freelance writer Teresa Mull contributed to this report.

title: Melinda French Gates says it took 3 doctors to diagnose the condition she was suffering from
summary: Melinda French Gates says it took three doctors to diagnose her perimenopause, revealing a startling gap in OB-GYN menopause training nationwide.
story: Dr. Amy Wechsler, a dual board-certified dermatologist and psychiatrist in Manhattan, reveals how she helps women who are battling acne as they age.
Melinda French Gates is speaking out about the challenges of recognizing perimenopause, saying she didn't receive the proper diagnosis and treatment until after seeing three different doctors.
She shared her experience with journalist Norah O'Donnell's new podcast "Healthful," which will be released on Wednesday.
French Gates, now 61, said she was in her early 40s when she began experiencing menopause symptoms, noting that she "kind of couldn't believe it," as reported by CBS News.
LOW TESTOSTERONE? HEGSETH SPARKS CONVERSATION AS DOCTORS REVEAL WARNING SIGNS EVERY MAN SHOULD KNOW
Later, the philanthropist and businesswoman would learn that many OB-GYNs receive little formal training in menopause care, which she says underscores a broader gap in women's healthcare.

Melinda French Gates is speaking out about the challenges of recognizing perimenopause, saying she didn't receive the proper diagnosis and treatment until after seeing three different doctors. (Getty Images)
French Gates shared that she was lucky enough to know the signs, thanks to input from older friends.

"But it was kind of unbelievable to me that, even in this, you know, unbelievably privileged situation I'm in, where I feel like I can get some of the best healthcare, it took me three doctors to really diagnose what I was going through and to get the right treatments for where I was," she said during the interview.
TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ
"It wasn't because anybody was doing the wrong thing. It's because of what I now know, which is, only one-third of OB-GYNs in this country are trained in menopause."

Supporting her claim, a national survey published in the journal Menopause in 2023 found that only about one-third of U.S. obstetrics and gynecology residency programs include a formal menopause curriculum.
More recently, a 2024 study found that OB-GYN, family medicine and internal medicine residents have low knowledge and low confidence in treating menopausal symptoms.

"It wasn't because anybody was doing the wrong thing. It's because of what I now know, which is, only one-third of OB-GYNs in this country are trained in menopause," French Gates told journalist Norah O'Donnell on her podcast "Healthful." (Getty Images)

In a separate 2026 Kansas study, more than half of residents reported receiving fewer than five hours of menopause education — and the majority did not believe that residency fully prepared them to treat menopausal patients independently.
In a national survey of 2,000 women, only 25% said their healthcare provider had adequately informed them about perimenopause.

Additional training in this area could help, researchers claim, as knowledge scores increased from 61% to 79% among those who received a structured curriculum.
About 1.3 million U.S. women reach menopause each year, according to The Menopause Society. Most begin perimenopause in their 40s, although it can start earlier. (Getty Images)
About 1.3 million U.S. women reach menopause each year, according to The Menopause Society. Most begin perimenopause in their 40s, although it can start earlier.

As perimenopause causes hormone levels to fluctuate, women can experience a range of symptoms. Some of the most common include irregular periods, hot flashes, night sweats, sleep disturbances, mood changes, vaginal dryness, brain fog and joint pain as hormone levels begin to fluctuate, according to Mayo Clinic.

title: NYC Legionnaires' disease outbreak kills fourth victim, 76 cases reported
summary: A fourth person has died as 76 Legionnaires' disease cases are now linked to cooling towers in Upper East Side buildings, including the Guggenheim Museum.
story: NYC health officials warn residents of a Legionnaires' disease outbreak with 23 confirmed cases. Dr. Stephanie Widmer explains the bacterial pneumonia, its symptoms like cough and fever, and its curability.
An outbreak of Legionnaires' disease in New York City killed a fourth person as 76 cases have now been reported in the city, city health authorities announced Monday.

The outbreak, which city authorities have linked to a series of cooling towers in Upper East Side buildings, has hospitalized 60 people, 53 of whom were discharged while seven remained in the hospital, according to authorities.
The fourth death announced Monday follows a first death from the disease on Friday. City officials announced two additional deaths over the weekend.
DEADLY LEGIONNAIRES' DISEASE OUTBREAK SPARKS CONCERN IN MAJOR US CITY: KNOW THE SYMPTOMS

Legionnaires disease comes from live Legionella bacteria infecting a person's lungs. While, according to New York City health authorities, most people exposed to the bacteria don't get sick, infection can cause a severe form of pneumonia that can be fatal.
Michigan reported an uptick in Legionnaires' disease.   (iStock)

"Symptoms typically develop two to fourteen days after exposure and include fever, chills, muscle aches, shortness of breath, and cough. Legionnaires’ disease can be effectively treated with antibiotics when diagnosed early," New York City's Health Department wrote in a statement.
City officials discovered the recent outbreak on July 2, and quickly tied it to a series of cooling towers in 31 different buildings in the city.
NYC HEALTH OFFICIALS WARN CENTRAL PARK VISITORS AFTER LEGIONNAIRES’ OUTBREAK GROWS ON UPPER EAST SIDE

summary: Fitness influencer Clavicular told Sean Hannity he secretly ordered testosterone at age 14, calling natural weightlifting a "complete waste of time."
story: Internet personality Clavicular joins ‘Hang Out with Sean Hannity’ to explain his controversial health regimen aimed at maximizing his facial appearance.
Clavicular revealed on the "Hang Out with Sean Hannity" podcast that he abandoned natural weightlifting as a teenager in favor of taking testosterone.
