"I will work to build a new politics; the country is crying out for it," he said Friday. "People are looking for us to deliver, and we will."
Reuters and Fox News' Efrat Lachter contributed to this report.

Eric Mack is a breaking news reporter and writer Sunday through Thursday, 6 a.m. ET to 2 p.m. ET, with a particular interest in stories that lead the news cycle on politics, elections, foreign affairs and government.

title: Steve Forbes urges Trump to keep the Strait of Hormuz open at all costs
summary: Publisher Steve Forbes calls for maximum pressure on Tehran regime, urges Trump administration to keep the Strait of Hormuz open as a non-negotiable imperative.
story: Publisher Steve Forbes argues the Strait of Hormuz is a strategic asset that must remain open at all costs, advises Trump to keep all options on the table in dealing with Iran
Steve Forbes says the United States must double down on efforts to topple the Tehran regime, arguing that free passage through the Strait of Hormuz should remain a non-negotiable American imperative.

As the U.S. struck targets in Iran for a ninth consecutive day on Sunday, pressure on the Tehran regime continued to build. Speaking at Freedom Fest in Las Vegas, the chairman and editor-in-chief of Forbes and former presidential candidate sat down with Fox News Digital to discuss Iran and the Trump administration's foreign policy.
STEVE FORBES BACKS TRUMP'S MT. RUSHMORE WARNING ON COMMUNISM: 'HE'S RIGHT'
"Get Iran done with. No more fake ceasefires. Get rid of that evil regime," Steve Forbes said. (Fox News)

"Going back to Thomas Jefferson, a core foreign policy plank of the United States is freedom of the seas. Freedom of navigation got us into another war with Great Britain, the War of 1812," Forbes said.
"So we've been doing it for over two centuries. The Strait of Hormuz is an international waterway, just as the South China Sea is an international waterway. And so we must keep that open.

August 1804: Tracers arc in the sky as ships of the U.S. navy bombard Tripoli in an action against a ruler who supported the Tripolitan (Barbary) pirates. The pirates demanded protection money from all ships and the USA decided to go to war to release their hold on the area.  (MPI/Getty Images)
"No tolls, no restrictions, all ships of commerce should have free passage through it unmolested."

Forbes said that with proper application of air power, boots on the ground wouldn't be needed, but he would not discard that as an option, bringing the example of the engagement with the Barbary pirates, which brought freedom of navigation to the Mediterranean following the completion of the First Barbary War of 1805.
TWO US SERVICE MEMBERS KILLED IN IRANIAN STRIKES ON JORDAN, CENTCOM SAYS
The U.S. military has been enforcing a naval blockade in the Strait of Hormuz, even during the ceasefire. (U.S. Central Command)

"If we do things right in the air, that won't be necessary. But as we demonstrated with the Barbary pirates, sometimes you do need hand-to-hand combat. But again, with our great military and the great Israeli military, we should be able to bring this evil regime down and enable the elements in the Iranian army that want change to feel we're not going to pull the rug out from under them with another fake ceasefire. That we keep hammering away at this evil regime."
A container ship, right, and a cargo vessel are seen in the Strait of Hormuz off Bandar Abbas, Iran, June 17, 2026. (Amirhosein Khorgooi/ISNA via AP)
Ultimately, Forbes said freedom of navigation should be an international red line:

"So the key thing is, if you don't enforce these key principles of freedom of navigation, liberty, you're going to lose them. Ronald Reagan was right. Others have made the same observation. You have to preserve liberty each and every generation."
President Ronald Reagan gives a speech from the Oval Office of the White House. (Diana Walker/Getty Images)
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
Forbes said the time for diplomacy with Tehran has passed, and encouraged the Trump administration to ratchet up the pressure, while also praising a recent decision on Ukraine policy.

"Get Iran done with. No more fake ceasefires. Get rid of that evil regime. By the way, I'm delighted that he's saying he's going to give licensing for Patriot missiles to Ukraine. That'll bring a good result there."
David Unsworth reports on Latin America. You can follow David Unsworth on Twitter @LatinAmerUpdate

title: Ex-counterterrorism official Joe Kent continues calling for US military withdrawal from Middle East
summary: Former National Counterterrorism Center Director Joe Kent is continuing to advocate for the withdrawal of U.S. forces from the Middle East.
story: 'The Big Weekend Show' co-hosts discuss CENTCOM's announcement of a ninth straight night of strikes against Iran.
Former National Counterterrorism Center Director Joe Kent is reiterating his call for the withdrawal of US forces from the Middle East amid the ongoing war with Iran.

"Get our troops out now before we suffer a mass casualty attack. Break the escalation trap. Trump still has the political strength at home to declare victory & have it resonate, that ability will be lost if we suffer more casualties. Now is the time to leave, immediately," he wrote Sunday on X.
Kent made the comments while sharing a post from U.S. Central Command (CENTCOM).

"Yesterday, U.S. Central Command (CENTCOM) announced the passing of two U.S. service members and the missing status of one in Jordan following an Iranian attack on July 17. After a thorough search, U.S. military personnel found unidentified remains at the location earlier today. An examination process to verify the remains is ongoing," CENTCOM noted in part of a statement on Sunday.

"Separately, a U.S. service member in northern Iraq was killed in action July 18 during a controlled detonation of unexploded ordnance from a downed Iranian one-way attack drone. A second service member was wounded and continues to receive medical treatment for a minor injury," the statement noted.
US SERVICE MEMBER KILLED IN IRAQ AS TROOPS RECOVER UNIDENTIFIED REMAINS IN JORDAN: CENTCOM
President Donald Trump steps off Air Force One upon arrival at John F. Kennedy International Airport in New York, N.Y. on July 17, 2026. (Mandel NGAN / AFP via Getty Images)
A White House spokesperson on Monday pointed Fox News Digital to comments President Donald Trump had made on Sunday.
"Well, we feel very badly. But you know those great people, those great patriots were out there fighting that Iran cannot have a nuclear weapon," he said.

"Iran has been very, very badly damaged," he said, asserting that the foreign nation has "lost everything, almost, militarily. They've got very little left. They've got some missiles.  They've got some drones.  They've got some manufacturing ability — not much," he said. "We control the Strait.  They don't control anything.  So we'll see what happens. But we hit 'em very hard again tonight," he said, adding that "we did that in honor of the probably three — it’s probably three, as opposed to two — great patriots."
EX-COUNTERTERRORISM OFFICIAL JOE KENT ENDORSES GOP SENATE PRIMARY CHALLENGER AS TRUMP BACKS LINDSEY GRAHAM
Kent quit the counterterrorism government post earlier this year, citing his opposition to the Iran war.
In part of his resignation letter he asserted, "Iran posed no imminent threat to our nation, and it is clear that we started this war due to pressure from Israel and its powerful American lobby."
EX-COUNTERTERRORISM CHIEF WARNS OF 'MAJOR PROBLEM' THAT COULD FORCE US 'BACK INTO THE WAR ON IRAN'S TERMS'

Joseph Kent, director of the National Counterterrorism Center, during a House Homeland Security Committee hearing in Washington, D.C., on Thursday, Dec. 11, 2025. (Daniel Heuer/Bloomberg via Getty Images)
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

In a portion of a Saturday post on X he wrote, "We restore order by ending the conflict on our terms: deprive Iran of military targets to strike by removing our troops, bases, & naval forces from the area. Our bases in the region are liabilities & relics of the past—abandoning them is not retreat, it’s strategic adaptation to modern warfare. This move removes Iran’s primary justification for disrupting shipping in the SOH and for attacking its neighbors. We can then offer the carrot: sanctions relief in exchange for freedom of navigation in the SOH."
Alex Nitzberg is a writer for Fox News Digital.

title: ISIS poised to exploit historic US Iraq exit, terror group 'actively waiting in the gaps,' expert warns
summary: ISIS fighters in Syria may have grown from 2,000 to 10,000 as the U.S. prepares to complete its Iraq withdrawal by Sept. 30, an expert warns.
story: President Donald Trump announced U.S. troops will leave Iraq by the end of September, ending a 23-year presence.

The Islamic State is quietly rebuilding as the United States prepares to complete its withdrawal from Iraq, raising fears the terror group could exploit a security vacuum, a regional security expert warned Sunday.

With U.S. forces leaving by Sept. 30 and as Baghdad tries to rein in Iran-backed militias, Iraq could also be entering its most dangerous period since ISIS seized Mosul in 2014, according to counterterrorism expert Dr. Omar Mohammed.
"ISIS is waiting actively in the gaps, as it historically always has," Mohammed, author and researcher with the George Washington University Program on Extremism, told Fox News Digital.
US SERVICE MEMBER KILLED IN IRAQ AS TROOPS RECOVER UNIDENTIFIED REMAINS IN JORDAN: CENTCOM
The Islamic State is quietly rebuilding as the United States prepares to complete its withdrawal from Iraq, regional analysts say. (History/Universal Images Group via Getty Images)
"The question is not whether American forces leave Iraq in September; that timetable is set. The question is what leaves with them."
"The militias claim the ISIS threat in order to keep their weapons, while ISIS recruits from the grievances that the militias create," Mohammed explained.
"That is exactly the dynamic that hollowed out Mosul before 2014, when the city was caught between a sectarian security apparatus and the insurgency it fed."
After preparing for years, ISIS captured Mosul, about 250 miles north of Baghdad, over a decade ago. Iraqi security forces collapsed and fled the city.

The group built underground networks through assassinations, extortion, intimidation and infiltration before launching its offensive. ISIS seized U.S.-made weapons and hundreds of millions of dollars before leader Abu Bakr al-Baghdadi declared the group's self-proclaimed caliphate.
At the time, Mohammed launched "Mosul Eye," a blog that secretly documented life under ISIS rule, exposing its operations and offering intelligence to U.S. forces.
TRUMP ADMIN WARNS IRAQ OVER IRAN TERROR PROXIES AS US REPORTEDLY BLOCKS CASH PAYMENTS
U.S. Central Command (CENTCOM) has said it will continue working to dismantle ISIS networks and prevent the terror group's resurgence. (AHMAD AL-RUBAYE/AFP via Getty Images)

Mohammed’s story is chronicled in Mosul Eye: A Scholar's Clandestine War Against ISIS, out July 21 from Skyhorse Publishing, with a foreword by Pope Francis and an introduction by retired Gen. David Petraeus.
Iraqi forces, backed by the U.S.-led coalition, went on to recapture Mosul in July 2017. When the U.S. combat mission ended in 2021, ISIS continued operating in parts of Iraq and Syria.
U.S. Central Command (CENTCOM) has said it will continue working to dismantle ISIS networks and prevent the terror group's resurgence.

But, citing Iraqi intelligence estimates, Mohammed said the number of ISIS fighters in neighboring Syria has increased from around 2,000 to as many as 10,000 since the collapse of Bashar Assad's government in 2024.
Mohammed also said the Popular Mobilization Forces, or PMF, an umbrella organization integrated into Iraq's security forces, was never disbanded after ISIS's territorial defeat.

He estimated the force has about 238,000 members, receives billions of dollars in government funding and includes factions with close ties to Iran that operate outside the Iraqi government's direct control.
IRAN TARGETS US WITH PSYCHOLOGICAL WARFARE CAMPAIGN TO MANIPULATE AMERICANS, EMBARRASS TRUMP: EXPERTS

With U.S. forces leaving by Sept. 30 and as Baghdad tries to rein in Iran-backed militias, Iraq could also be entering its most dangerous period since ISIS seized Mosul in 2014. (REUTERS/Mohammed Ameen)
Now Baghdad is trying to bring armed factions, including Kataib Hezbollah and Asaib Ahl al-Haq, under full state control.
"Sept. 30 is not one deadline; it is two," Mohammed said, referring to the simultaneous U.S. withdrawal and the domestic disarmament push.
"The militias and ISIS are not separate stories; they are deeply interdependent. Each actively justifies the other. Both forces thrive in the unstable spaces the central state cannot hold."

The U.S. withdrawal also follows a 2024 U.S.-Iraq agreement that envisioned ending the mission in Iraq by 2025 while continuing support for anti-ISIS operations in Syria through September 2026. Mohammed warned against repeating past complacency.

"Mosul did not fall in 2014 because ISIS was strong. It fell because everything that would have detected its strength—presence, attention, honest reporting from the ground—had been withdrawn in the years before, while the world's eyes were elsewhere."
I'VE STUDIED MILITARY STRATEGY. TRUMP NOW FACES IRAN'S OLDEST BATTLEFIELD TRICK

U.S. President Donald Trump gestures toward Iraqi Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi as they participate in a bilateral meeting in the Oval Office at the White House in Washington, D.C., U.S., July 14, 2026. (Evan Vucci/Reuters)
Meanwhile, Iraqi Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi’s White House meeting July 14, where it was announced remaining U.S. troops would leave Iraq, drew condemnation from Tehran.
According to Iran International, Ali Akbar Velayati, an adviser to Iran's Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei , called al-Zaidi's trip "regrettable" and claimed it damaged Iraq's dignity.
Mohammed said Iran's influence inside Iraq is important to Tehran after U.S. strikes degraded parts of its proxy network.

"Iran's strategic calculation matters more now than at any point in a decade because Iraq is essentially what Iran has left," Mohammed said. "So the regime's real fear is not resurgence. It is irrelevance."

Tehran fears an Iraq where the government successfully disarms the militias, U.S. forces leave on Baghdad's terms rather than Iran's, and no active security crisis remains to justify armed groups operating outside full state control, he said.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
"That said, what happens across the wider region after September will not be decided by anyone's stated intentions or diplomatic promises," Mohammed added.

"I have seen what a city pays when that judgment is wrong. Whether ISIS grows large enough to frighten Iran, or stays just large enough to serve it, will be one of the defining questions of the year after the withdrawal," he warned.
Fox News Digital has reached out to the White House for comment.

Emma Bussey is a breaking news writer for Fox News Digital. Before joining Fox, she worked at The Telegraph with the U.S. overnight team, across desks including foreign, politics, news, sport and culture.

title: 'We want land invasion': Iran mouthpiece touts new missile, boasts decades of war prep
summary: Regime mouthpiece Seyed Mohammad Marandi claims Iran welcomes a U.S. ground invasion and has introduced a new missile as strikes hit Khorramabad.
story: U.S. Central Command reported forces hit ‘surveillance sites, military logistics infrastructure, underground weapons storage and maritime capabilities’ as it continues its strikes on Iran.

Tehran has spent decades preparing for — and welcoming — a U.S. ground invasion, a senior Iranian official has claimed, as fresh explosions rocked the region on the eighth day of renewed U.S.-Iran strikes.

Seyed Mohammad Marandi, an Iranian American academic identified as a regime "mouthpiece," also boasted that Tehran had just launched a "new missile" while decentralizing and burying its arsenal deep underground to withstand sustained American air campaigns.

"The Americans are planning an invasion. I'm not saying it will necessarily happen. I'm not saying it will necessarily happen in the next few days. But they have plans for an invasion," Marandi, who served as an advisor to Iran's nuclear negotiation team during recent talks with the U.S. in Pakistan, said in an interview with political analyst Glenn Diesen.
I'VE STUDIED MILITARY STRATEGY. TRUMP NOW FACES IRAN'S OLDEST BATTLEFIELD TRICK
Seyed Mohammad Marandi, an Iranian American academic frequently identified as a regime "mouthpiece," said Tehran had recently launched a new missile. (Akila Jayawardena/NurPhoto via Getty Images)

"Whether they carry them out or not, we'll see. But the Iranians, as you pointed out, the focus of Iranian strikes is on Bahrain and Kuwait, and that's because that's where most American assets have been placed for a ground invasion," Diesen said.
Marandi’s comments came as the conflict expanded across western and southern Iran in the run-up to Saturday.
Iran also launched missile and drone salvos targeting U.S.-linked facilities in Jordan, Kuwait and Bahrain.
Jordanian officials confirmed they intercepted 10 missiles early Saturday, while authorities in Kuwait reported casualties and severe damage to a domestic power and desalination plant.
In response, U.S. airstrikes struck bridges, a key road tunnel, surveillance outposts and reinforced underground weapons storage facilities.

Multiple explosions also rocked the city of Khorramabad in Iran's Lorestan province. Iranian state media claimed the blasts were caused by U.S. missiles launched from regional bases in Kuwait, according to reports.
TRUMP SAYS IRAN'S MISSILES 'AREN'T THE PROBLEM' AFTER WHITE HOUSE MADE THEM CENTRAL TO WAR RATIONALE
Satellite image shows the second tunnel entrance and support buildings at the Khorramabad missile complex in Lorestan province, Iran, before March airstrikes. (Vantor/Unknown)

Khorramabad houses the Imam Ali Missile Base, one of Tehran's primary underground silo facilities engineered to store and deploy liquid-fueled Shahab-3 medium-range ballistic missiles, according to Washington’s Nuclear Threat Initiative.
The complex was damaged by Israeli airstrikes during the 2025 campaign targeting Tehran's military and nuclear infrastructure.
Marandi also detailed what he described as a resilient, subterranean network central to Tehran's military strategy.

"When Iran wants to fire missiles or drones, they don't put them inside buildings or in piles somewhere. They take out whatever they need," Marandi said. "They fire them, and then they go back to their bases, or they take out different missiles and drones, spread them out in different areas, put them apart from one another so that the Americans cannot bomb them in large numbers."
He added: "Everything has been spread out in Iran and placed underground."
The latest escalation between the U.S. and Iran ended a recently signed memorandum of understanding (MOU) to establish a 60-day ceasefire and facilitate nuclear talks.
The key issue has centered on control of the Strait of Hormuz, with the strategic waterway turning into the conflict's main battleground.
TRUMP'S 60-DAY IRAN DEAL REACHES HALFWAY MARK AS CEASEFIRE COLLAPSES INTO ESCALATING WAR
Marandi claimed that the IRCG introduced a new missile to the war. (Morteza Nikoubazl/NurPhoto via Getty Images)
President Donald Trump ordered renewed airstrikes within weeks of the truce, or MOU, being implemented, and on July 14, he floated the possibility of launching a ground campaign.
According to Marandi, Iran's military command is actively counting on a ground scenario and has since introduced a new weapon to the theater.
"Iran has that advantage, and of course, it has been accumulating missiles and drones for decades now, and it is doing so even now," Marandi claimed.
"They, I think, last night introduced a new missile to the war," he said of the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRCG).
"The Iranians are hitting very hard, and they are prepared for a land war. They've been preparing for decades."
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
Marandi concluded by claiming that Tehran views a U.S. ground operation as the most direct path to ending the conflict on its own terms.

"The Iranians — we discussed this during the 40-day war before on your show — when I said that the Iranians actually want the Americans to carry out a land invasion, and the same is true now, because they felt that if there was a land invasion, they would win," he told Diesen.

Emma Bussey is a breaking news writer for Fox News Digital. Before joining Fox, she worked at The Telegraph with the U.S. overnight team, across desks including foreign, politics, news, sport and culture.

title: US service member killed in Iraq as troops recover unidentified remains in Jordan: CENTCOM
summary: A U.S. service member was killed in Iraq while handling explosives from a downed Iranian drone as troops searching in Jordan recovered unidentified remains.
story: President Donald Trump monitors events in Iran as U.S. forces conduct a seventh night of strikes on military and logistics infrastructure. Fox News reporter Alex Hogan reports the latest and Fox News contributor Mike Pompeo weighs in.
A U.S. service member was killed Saturday during an operation involving explosive remnants from a downed Iranian drone in northern Iraq, U.S. Central Command (CENTCOM) announced Sunday.
A second U.S. service member was also wounded in the incident, officials said.
The announcement came as CENTCOM confirmed unidentified remains were found Sunday during the search for a U.S. service member reported missing in Jordan following a separate Iranian attack on Friday.
TWO US SERVICE MEMBERS KILLED IN IRANIAN STRIKES ON JORDAN, CENTCOM SAYS
An Arleigh Burke-class guided-missile destroyer USS Thomas Hudner fires a Tomahawk land attack missile in support of Operation Epic Fury March 1, 2026. (U.S. Navy via Getty Images)
According to officials, the incident in Iraq happened after U.S. forces recovered a downed Iranian drone and began handling the explosive material left behind.
"A U.S. service member in northern Iraq was killed in action July 18 during a controlled detonation of unexploded ordnance from a downed Iranian one-way attack drone," CENTCOM wrote in a post on X.
LEAKED IRAN REPORT FINDS RECORD PUBLIC ANGER AS REGIME FOCUSES ON HOLDING POWER
Iran coordinates mass drone warfare campaign across Middle East targeting Western sites. (Getty Images )
The military did not immediately release further details about the incident, but said the other service member injured in the operation is receiving medical treatment.
In Jordan, officials said the unidentified remains recovered Sunday will also undergo an examination to determine their identity.
"After a thorough search, U.S. military personnel found unidentified remains at the location earlier today," CENTCOM said. "An examination process to verify the remains is ongoing."

A billboard depicting Iran's supreme leaders since 1979: (L to R) Ayatollahs Ruhollah Khomeini (until 1989), Ali Khamenei (until 2026), and Mojtaba Khamenei (current) is displayed above a highway in Tehran on March 10, 2026.  (AFP/Via Getty Images)
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
Friday's Iranian attack on a U.S. base in Jordan killed two U.S. service members, CENTCOM previously said.
Four American service members were also medically evacuated to Jordanian hospitals, officials said. They have since been discharged.
"CENTCOM is withholding additional information, including the identities of the missing and fallen warriors, out of respect for the families during the notification process," the agency said.
This is a developing story. Please check back for updates.
Bonny Chu is a Breaking and Trending News Writer for Fox News Digital

title: Netanyahu fires back at NYC Mayor Mamdani's vow to enforce 'bogus arrest warrant'
summary: Benjamin Netanyahu's office accuses Zohran Mamdani of attacking the Jewish state to distract from the damage his policies have caused New York.
story: New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani said Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu is a 'war criminal' during a New York Times interview.

Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's office is accusing New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani of attacking the Jewish state to distract from his record in New York after calling Netanyahu a "war criminal."

The prime minister's office fired back Sunday after the Democratic mayor said his administration was exploring whether it could arrest the Israeli leader during an expected visit to the city under the International Criminal Court's warrant.

"The ICC is a kangaroo court that has no jurisdiction over Americans or Israelis," Netanyahu's office wrote in an X post Sunday, amid recent reports he is nearing a trip to the White House to meet with President Donald Trump.
POTENTIAL 2028 DEM CONTENDER UNLOADS ON NETANYAHU, ADMITS US-ISRAEL TIES AT 'CROSSROADS'
New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani has threatened to enforce the International Criminal Court's arrest warrant on Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu. (Getty Images)

"Its bogus arrest warrant against Prime Minister Netanyahu was issued by a disgraced former ICC Prosecutor, Karim Khan, a few days before allegations of sexual misconduct against him became public," Netanyahu's office said. "It was a clear attempt by Khan to divert public attention and seek protection from scrutiny."
Mamdani is following the same playbook, the office added.

"Instead of backing Khan's criminal behaviour, Mr. Mamdani should focus on fixing the damage his policies have caused New York," the post concluded. "Like Karim Khan, Mamdani appears interested in diverting public attention from his follies and attacking the leader of the Jewish state and the only democracy in the Middle East."
MAMDANI SPARKS FIERCE BACKLASH FOR WORLD CUP STUNT 'PALLING AROUND' WITH RIKERS ISLAND CONVICTS
Israel vowed to ignore the ICC warrant while it roots Hamas, "a genocidal terrorist organization ," out of Gaza.

"Under Prime Minister Netanyahu's leadership, Israel has taken unprecedented wartime measures to minimize harm to civilians while confronting Hamas, a genocidal terrorist organization that uses Palestinians as human shields and deliberately targets innocent Israeli civilians," the office's post read.
Former Secretary of State Mike Pompeo told Fox News' "Fox & Friends Weekend" earlier Sunday that Mamdani is ostensibly hyperbolizing for "political theater."

"This is a communist, antisemitic mayor trying to make news for his own audience," Pompeo said. "There's nothing more than that. This is no chance he's going to arrest Prime Minister Netanyahu when he comes to New York in September for the U.N. General Assembly.
"It's just simply not going to happen, and he knows it."
Even some Democrats have rejected Mamdani's stance, warning it could embolden terrorists at home and abroad.
"This isn’t a college protest," former Democrat Mayor Eric Adams wrote on X. "This is the City of New York."

"Threatening to arrest the democratically elected leader of one of America’s closest allies during U.N. General Assembly week isn’t bold. It’s reckless," Adams continued. "American diplomats, service members, and officials are stationed in dangerous places around the world. Irresponsible rhetoric like this doesn’t stay in New York. It can put Americans at greater risk abroad. Leadership means understanding that your words have consequences. Reckless political theater can have very real-world costs."
Sen. John Fetterman, D-Pa., has long broken with Democrats on becoming the "anti-Israel party," telling the "clown" Mamdani to "sit down."
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

"It's such a tough guy to say that kind of thing," Fetterman told Fox News' "Sunday Morning Futures." "He has no way to do that, of course. Obviously, America is not even part of that corrupt court. And so he's just a clown to even say that. So he won't try that. Just sit down and focus on other the problems that they have in New York. That's really not your purview. You and I know that. Sit down."

Eric Mack is a breaking news reporter and writer Sunday through Thursday, 6 a.m. ET to 2 p.m. ET, with a particular interest in stories that lead the news cycle on politics, elections, foreign affairs and government.

title: Earthquake shakes Peru's Andes region, killing at least 5, displacing hundreds
summary: A magnitude 5.5 earthquake near Sicaya killed at least five people and left hundreds homeless as adobe buildings collapsed across Peru's Andes region.
story: Fox News Flash top headlines are here. Check out what's clicking on FoxNews.com.

A powerful earthquake ripped through Peru's Andes region overnight, killing at least five people and leaving hundreds displaced as homes and a church collapsed, with authorities warning Sunday that an unknown number of people remain missing.

The magnitude 5.5 quake struck shortly after 9:20 p.m. Saturday near the city of Sicaya in central Peru, according to the U.S. Geological Survey. The quake injured more than 20 people and forced at least 300 residents from their homes, Peru's National Civil Defense Institute said.
Officials were still trying to account for missing residents Sunday after several buildings collapsed or were left unsafe, including a local church and convent.
SECURITY GUARD SURVIVES EIGHT DAYS BENEATH COLLAPSED SHOPPING CENTER AFTER VENEZUELA EARTHQUAKES
Residents walk amid the debris of homes that collapsed after an earthquake struck Pumpuya, Peru, Sunday, July 19, 2026. (AP Photo/Javier Ninanya)

Authorities said the region's widespread use of traditional adobe construction likely made the damage worse. Luis Vásquez, head of the local civil defense office, said the rustic building materials "contributed to the greater impact and damage."
A motor tricycle is stuck amid the debris of homes that collapsed after an earthquake struck Pumpuya, Peru, Sunday, July 19, 2026. (AP Photo/Jhefry Sedano)

Images from the hard-hit farming community of Chongo Bajo showed families wrapped in blankets outside damaged homes as neighbors picked through the rubble. Animals could also be seen trapped beneath collapsed buildings.
BOY, 2, PULLED ALIVE FROM RUBBLE SIX DAYS AFTER VENEZUELA'S DEVASTATING TWIN EARTHQUAKES
"My home has been destroyed," resident Hermenegilda Guamalato told local radio while looking for shelter with her three children in the neighboring province of Huayucachi.
Residents stand next to the covered bodies of neighbors who were killed after an earthquake struck Pumpuya, Peru, Sunday, July 19, 2026. (AP Photo/Javier Ninanya)
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
Peru sits along the Pacific "Ring of Fire," one of the world's most active earthquake zones. In 2007, a magnitude 7.9 earthquake struck the coastal province of Pisco, killing nearly 600 people.
The Associated Press contributed to this report.

title: Trump administration touts more than $1B in UN budget cuts as reform push gains momentum
summary: The Trump administration says it secured over $1 billion in U.N. budget cuts in six months, including a $550 million peacekeeping budget reduction.
story: U.S. Ambassador for U.N. Management and Reform Jeff Bartos is the official overseeing the Trump administration's U.N. reform agenda details more than $1 billion in spending cuts, a new approach to peacekeeping budgets and the next targets for reform.

UNITED NATIONS — The Trump administration says it has secured more than $1 billion in cuts to United Nations budgets in just six months, calling the reductions evidence that an institution long considered resistant to change is finally beginning to reform.

The latest milestone came June 30, when all 193 U.N. member states approved a peacekeeping budget of approximately $5.1 billion for the coming fiscal year — about $550 million, or 9.7%, less than the previous year.

Combined with a 15% reduction to the U.N.'s regular budget approved in December, U.S. officials say the agreements amount to more than $1 billion in cuts to assessed U.N. budgets, a level they describe as unprecedented.
INTERNATIONAL ‘DEEP STATE’ PRIME TARGET OF TRUMP-STYLE CANDIDATE FOR UN CHIEF
U.S. Representative for U.N. Ambassador Jeff Bartos addresses a meeting of the Security Council at U.N. headquarters in New York City, Nov. 25, 2025. (Eduardo Munoz/Reuters)
Assessed budgets are funded through mandatory contributions charged to member states under a formula based largely on the size of their economies.

"On June 30th, with U.S. leadership, all 193 countries came together again for the second time in six months," U.S. Ambassador for U.N. Management and Reform Jeff Bartos told Fox News Digital. "We've achieved over a billion dollars of savings in six months, which is unprecedented. Any one cut would be unprecedented. The totality of the reforms is monumental."

The agreement comes as the United Nations faces mounting financial pressure and prepares for a leadership transition in 2027, with Secretary-General António Guterres set to leave office at the end of his second term. At the same time, the Trump administration has made reform a central pillar of its U.N. strategy, arguing the organization has become overly bureaucratic and inefficient.

In response to questions from Fox News Digital, U.N. spokesman Stéphane Dujarric confirmed that the peacekeeping budget was reduced by roughly $550 million and the regular budget by 15%, describing both as "unprecedented reductions."
US URGES DONORS TO ABANDON UNRWA FUNDING AS UN DEFENDS AGENCY'S MISSION
A Cameroonian United Nations peacekeeping soldier guards women as they arrive to the village of Bambara, Central African Republic, April 25, 2017. (Reuters/Baz Ratner)
Bartos argues the reforms reflect sustained pressure from the Trump administration and months of negotiations led by the U.S. Mission.
"The new budget, this reformed budget, the enhanced efficiency changes the culture of how the U.N. looks at peacekeeping," Bartos said. "Every dollar has to achieve impact on the ground."
He pointed to the U.N. Mission in South Sudan as an example, saying the United States worked to streamline the mission's mandate before reducing its budget accordingly.
Another reform highlighted by the administration changes how the U.N. handles unused budget credits.

Until now, U.N. financial rules required the organization to return unspent funds to member states even if those contributions had never actually been paid, a practice critics said worsened the organization's recurring liquidity crisis.
The General Assembly voted on June 30 to introduce, on a four-year trial basis, a new methodology under which unspent funds will be returned only when backed by cash actually received.

Bartos said the change could save the organization more than $1 billion over the next three years. That projected figure is separate from the more than $1 billion in budget reductions already approved over the past six months.
He called the change another example of "common-sense" reform and said it could save the organization more than $1 billion over the next three years.
The United Nations likewise welcomed the change, though officials noted it had been a long-standing priority of Guterres.
TRUMP CELEBRATES AFTER UN CLIMATE COMMITTEE MOVES AWAY FROM ITS MOST EXTREME GLOBAL WARMING SCENARIO

President Donald Trump meets with Secretary-General António Guterres during the 80th session of the General Assembly at the United Nations headquarters on Sept. 23, 2025, in New York City. (Chip Somodevilla/Getty Images)

"I have been pushing for this reform for almost a decade," Guterres said after the vote. He described the previous system as a "Kafkaesque cycle" in which the organization was expected "to give back cash that did not exist."
Dujarric said the reform would allow the U.N. to manage resources "in a more predictable and responsible way" while helping ensure operational continuity, particularly for peacekeeping missions.
Bartos insists the latest budget agreements are only the beginning.

Among the administration's next priorities are reforms to staff compensation, employee benefits and the U.N. pension system, areas he argues consume resources that could otherwise support humanitarian operations and peacekeeping missions.

"We're going to continue to see us push whether it's on benefits, whether it's on staff compensation, whether it's on the pension system," Bartos said. "There's massive numbers of additional reforms that our team is working on right now."
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

Vehicles with the U.N. peacekeeping force in Lebanon drive along the main road leading to Lebanon's southern town of Naqura, close to the border with Israel, on Oct. 27, 2022. (Mahmoud Zayyat/AFP/Getty Images)
He also suggested reform will remain a central issue as member states begin selecting the next secretary-general.

"We're going to select the next secretary-general," Bartos said. "That reform momentum that has been growing over the last 15, 18 months... you'll see that continuing in 2027 with the new secretary-general."

Efrat (Effie) Lachter is an investigative journalist, filmmaker and war correspondent. She has directed and produced over 200 documentary segments across more than 40 countries. Recipient of the 2022 Peres Center for Peace Award, Lachter is also a 2023-24 Knight-Wallace Journalism Fellow at the University of Michigan. She holds a bachelor's degree in communication and a master's degree in political science.

The law, passed last year as part of the Trump administration’s “big, beautiful bill,” requires some Medicaid participants to work, volunteer or go to school for at least 80 hours each month. The requirements have already rolled out in some states, including Nebraska, and will be implemented across the country by Jan. 1.

title: Rep. Jim Jordan formally asks DOJ to prosecute Jack Smith over congressional testimony
summary: Jordan, chair of the House Judiciary Committee, accused Smith of lying in his testimony before the committee in December. Smith’s lawyers denied he made any false statements.
story: The top Republican on the House Judiciary Committee sent a letter to the Justice Department on Wednesday requesting a criminal investigation of former special counsel Jack Smith, alleging he made false statements during a congressional deposition last year.
Subscribe to read this story ad-free
Get unlimited access to ad-free articles and exclusive content.

Committee Chairman Jim Jordan, R-Ohio, wrote in a letter to acting Attorney General Todd Blanche that Smith “seemingly made willfully and intentionally false statements of material fact that contradict new documents” the Senate Judiciary Committee obtained this month.
Jordan asked the Justice Department to investigate Smith for a criminal charge, writing that his committee found “strong evidence” against him.
A spokesperson for the Justice Department confirmed receipt of the referral and said Wednesday that it “will investigate all evidence of criminal conduct.”
Smith has long been a target of President Donald Trump, who has disparaged him over his prosecutions of Trump.
Fox News first reported Jordan’s referral.

In a letter to Jordan and Blanche, attorneys for Smith denied that he made any false statements during his deposition, writing that he “provided truthful, responsive answers and candidly discussed his work as Special Counsel.”

“The referral is made not because Mr. Smith made a false statement — the letter concedes he did not — but because he did not proactively disclose information that was not responsive to a question asked,” lawyers Peter Koski and Lanny Breuer wrote.

The pair said the referral “reflects a chilling eagerness to weaponize the justice system by attacking a career, nonpartisan public servant who faithfully and fearlessly performed his duties by following the facts and the law.”

As special counsel, Smith oversaw two investigations beginning in 2022. One focused on election interference in the 2020 presidential election and the other on allegations that Trump mishandled classified documents after his first term ended. Trump denied any wrongdoing in both cases, which were dismissed in 2024 after he was elected to a second term. Longstanding DOJ policy prevents a sitting president from being prosecuted.
Jordan cited an exchange from Smith’s deposition before the committee on Dec. 17, when Smith was asked whether he sought a “search warrant for the content of any text messages from Members.”
Smith responded, “No, I don’t recall that.”
Asked whether he had asked only for toll records of the members of Congress, Smith said, “Correct.”

Rep. Jamie Raskin, D-Md., the ranking member of the committee, said in a statement Wednesday that Jordan’s referral “deliberately distorts and misstates the facts, including what questions the Republicans actually asked at Mr. Smith’s interview.”
“Congressional Republicans never asked Jack Smith about presidential records,” Raskin said.

Raskin argued that committee Republicans did not ask whether the messages from lawmakers were found on White House officials’ phones, whether the presidential records Smith subpoenaed included the messages or whether Smith’s team had ever “reviewed text messages from Members.”
“Jack Smith could not have lied because Republican Members never even asked the question their theory is based on,” he said.

Senate Republicans said last week that they had obtained documents from the Justice Department revealing Smith and his team reviewed text messages sent by 44 members of Congress as part of their investigations into Trump.

The documents the Senate Judiciary Committee obtained show that the messages were sent by lawmakers on both sides of the aisle, but mostly Republicans, to White House officials during Trump’s first term.

Smith’s team received the text messages from the National Archives and Records Administration in August 2023. They included text messages from October 2020 through Jan. 21, 2021, the committee said on July 14.

The Senate Judiciary Committee argued that because Smith’s team had not waited for a “Filter Team” to evaluate and segregate “privileged information” out of those messages, Smith and his team violated protections ensured by the Constitution’s Speech and Debate Clause.

“Smith’s team ran roughshod over the Constitution even after repeated warnings,” committee Chairman Chuck Grassley, R-Iowa, said in a statement on July 14. “Jack Smith has answering to do, and I intend to have him before the Senate Judiciary Committee in the coming months to hold him accountable.”
Grassley was on the list of members whose messages were reviewed, along with Jordan, former House Speaker Kevin McCarthy, R-Calif., and longtime Sens. John Cornyn, R-Texas, and Rand Paul, R-Ky.

title: The fight for the future of foldable phones is here
summary: Samsung has owned the market for foldable phones. Now Apple is getting in on it. NBC News chief tech analyst Joanna Stern breaks it down.
story: What’s the difference between a Samsung Galaxy Z Fold 8 Ultra, Fold 8 and Flip 8? Two fold, one flips and all three unfold your wallet. (Sorry.)
Subscribe to read this story ad-free
Get unlimited access to ad-free articles and exclusive content.

Making fun of Samsung’s product names is an old tradition. But what the company announced Wednesday is genuinely new and far more consequential than its usual summer foldable refresh. Apple is expected to unveil its first foldable iPhone in September, and RAM-ageddon continues to drive up all consumer electronics prices.

I spoke with one of Samsung’s top executives about Apple’s expected entry into the market and Samsung’s own seven-year head start. But first, let’s break down the differences among the three devices, so you don’t have to run the product names through a Samsung-to-human translator.
New shapes. Sure, there are small differences among the three phones, but shape is the biggest.
Galaxy Z Fold 8: The “all-new” Fold opens like a children’s book or a passport, revealing a wider main landscape display with a 4:3 aspect ratio. Think classic Hollywood. It starts at $1,900.

Galaxy Z Fold 8 Ultra: This one opens more like a tall pamphlet. It keeps the narrower, more vertical shape of Samsung’s previous Fold design. It also now has a ginormous battery. It starts at $2,100.
Galaxy Z Flip 8: This one folds vertically, like the flip phones of the early 2000s. It starts at $1,200.
All of these phones ship Aug. 7.

The most interesting is the new Galaxy Z Fold 8 — or what Samsung probably should have just called the Fold Widescreen. (Seriously, drop the Z, Samsung. The Z stands for “zero reason to keep it.”) It opens into a wider, more tablet-like display that’s better for watching videos. Apple’s first foldable iPhone is rumored to have a similar shape.

When I asked Drew Blackard, Samsung’s senior vice president of mobile product management, whether the Apple reports influenced the redesign, he said it was driven more by user experience. “Media consumption has really changed a lot since the first one we launched” in 2019, he said.
Samsung is keeping the taller Fold 8 Ultra around as a more productivity-focused device. In other words: one Fold for watching, another Fold for working and a Flip for pretending it’s 2005 again.

New prices. Blackard said the Fold 8 Ultra and the Flip 8 are each $100 more expensive than their predecessors. Both come with upgrades. The Ultra, for instance, has a larger battery — but he said rising RAM and storage costs were a “big driver” of the increases.
“It’s the big challenge right now,” he said, though he suggested many U.S. buyers may not feel the full hit as carriers launch deals and other creative ways to hide it in the bill.

New competitor. Looming over the entire announcement is Apple’s entry this fall. While Samsung has been betting for the last seven years on phones that expand into tablets, Apple will be making the same sell in whatever Apple way it devises.

Asked about the competition, Blackard touted the lead Samsung has in improving the durability, design and functionality. He also speculated that “they’ll probably have one form factor, and we’re excited to be offering three now.”
I don’t know, seems like only a matter of time until Apple gives us the iPhone Fold, Fold Pro and Fold Pro Max.

Joanna Stern is NBC News’ chief tech analyst and founder of New Things, a new independent media company that covers consumer technology. A version of this article first appeared in her New Things newsletter.

title: Wisconsin officer kills man armed with knife, police say, as shooting sparks protests
summary: Madison police said that after a chase and a struggle, a man who was being sought pulled out a knife and injured an officer, which led to the deadly shooting.
story: A police officer fatally shot a man who was alleged to have pulled out a knife during a struggle as officers were looking into a report of someone “checking vehicle doors” Wednesday afternoon in Madison, Wisconsin, police said.
Subscribe to read this story ad-free
Get unlimited access to ad-free articles and exclusive content.

Police responded to the Marquette neighborhood about 1 p.m. after a report of someone checking parked cars, Madison Police Chief John Patterson said at a news conference. The person fled on a bicycle, but officers re-encountered him around 1:35 p.m., Patterson said.
The man “either fell off or was taken off of the bicycle by officers,” and there was a struggle with police in the intersection, Patterson said.
“During the struggle, the man, we’re told, pulled out a knife or produced a knife, a fixed-blade knife, and an officer was injured by this while attempting to arrest him,” Patterson said.
The police department included a photo showing a knife on the ground in a news release about the deadly encounter.
Patterson said that a stun gun was used during the struggle but that it was not effective and that the officer who was injured by the knife was the officer who fired his gun.

Videos of the shooting were captured by bystanders and were circulated online. One of them, verified by NBC News, appears to show officers holding on to the man as someone yells, “Let go!” Multiple shouts of “He’s got a knife!” can be heard.

The video also shows what appears to be an officer yelling “Taser!” as the man stands while being held by police. About three seconds later, while the man is on the ground, a male officer standing over him appears to fire three rounds, and the man stops moving.
Patterson said that he has seen some videos but added that other video has not been circulated online and is being reviewed.
“I caution everyone — this is one perspective,” Patterson said. “It is not a full overview of everything that was visible from different angles, certainly visible from the officers.”
The shooting was not captured on body camera video, which the Madison Police Department does not widely use.
“We do not have body cameras on any of the officers involved,” Patterson said.

There was a 90-day body camera pilot program for the department in 2024, NBC affiliate WMTV of Madison reported at the time. Patterson has pushed for the cameras, calling them an “essential tool” for modern policing last month, local TV station WKOW reported, but funding has been an issue.
The person who was killed was not identified at Wednesday’s news conference. He was described as a man in his 30s.
“I want to take a moment to honestly and sincerely offer my heartfelt sympathies to his family for this loss,” Patterson said.
The police officer who fired was also not identified. Patterson said the officer is a man and “is what I would consider a veteran officer.”
Madison Council Alder Davy Mayer, who represents the district where the shooting took place, said he was in contact with city officials and police about the incident.
“My priority is to make sure the community remains safe and that the public receives full details about what happened as soon as possible,” Mayer said.
All four officers at the scene will be placed on administrative leave, which Patterson said was routine practice after a shooting involving police.
Michael Doubek, who recorded one of the videos showing the shooting, said he was returning from a co-op grocery store on Williamson Street when he saw police cruisers “flying by.”
Doubek said the officers were struggling to restrain the person on the ground when one of the officers fired.
Doubek said that after the person was shot, he saw police toss a knife to the side as officers surrounded the person on the ground.

Video from a Milwaukee Journal Sentinel reporter showed a large group of protesters walking down a street Wednesday evening. The Wisconsin Chamber Orchestra announced that a planned outdoor performance had been canceled.
Police said that the state Department of Justice Division of Criminal Investigation will conduct an independent investigation and that the district attorney will conduct a review.

The Wisconsin Department of Justice said that its Division of Criminal Investigation is leading the investigation but that it is being assisted by the Dane County Sheriff’s Office, the Wisconsin State Patrol and the Sun Prairie Police Department.
“Involved law enforcement are fully cooperating with DCI during this investigation,” the state justice department said.
Madison Mayor Satya Rhodes-Conway said she was “angered and saddened by what happened today.”

“Any officer-involved shooting needs to be rigorously investigated, and this one will be,” Rhodes-Conway said in a statement. “While we do not yet know all the details, our community deserves full transparency and accountability.”
Gov. Tony Evers said he’s been briefed and expressed his condolences to the man’s family.

“There must be transparency and accountability in any investigation moving forward,” Evers said on X. “We will continue to keep the loved ones and family of the individual who was killed in our hearts and prayers. His life mattered.”

title: ‘Off the charts’: Secret Service describes rising threats to protectees
summary: Despite the heightened environment, the Secret Service says it’s confident in plans for the rescheduled White House Correspondents’ Association dinner.
story: WASHINGTON — The Secret Service has opened more than 10,000 investigations this year into threats against people it protects, a 40% rise over the same period last year, officials said Wednesday.
Subscribe to read this story ad-free
Get unlimited access to ad-free articles and exclusive content.
Director Sean Curran told reporters at a briefing that the volatile political climate has reached a new level that he has not seen in his 24-year career.
He said the threat numbers are “off the charts.”

Despite the heightened environment — President Donald Trump has been the target of at least three assassination attempts — Curran and other senior leaders at the agency tasked with protecting Trump and other high-profile politicians are confident in security plans ahead of the rescheduled White House Correspondents’ Association dinner this week.

In April, a gunman stormed a security checkpoint, fired on an officer and was subdued before he reached the ballroom in Washington where Trump, the first lady, Cabinet officials and more than 2,600 journalists and other guests were in attendance.
Friday’s event will be held at a different Washington hotel with a much smaller ballroom and fewer guests. Trump is expected to attend and speak.
Curran said law enforcement is prepared.
“We will always evaluate every site. And right now, we have an advance team there, and they will take back and they will set up a plan to set that site up for success,” he said.
Deputy Director Matthew Quinn said the agency does not see a shadow cast by the April incident.

“We’re not looking at this as a redo of a dinner,” he said. “We’re looking at this as a presidential site with Cabinet members and other protectees there, just like every site we do everywhere we go.”
Curran said the security perimeter at the Washington Hilton worked because the gunman was kept a significant distance from Trump.
“We’re talking almost 120 yards from magnetometers to podium. That’s over a football field,” he said.
Beyond planning for Friday’s high-profile event, officials provided new insights about another emerging threat: drones.

The foiled plot to attack the June UFC fights at the White House included use of drones, according to court documents. Officials said they are deploying new detection methods around the White House and when the president travels.
“We’re also moving these assets around with the president, some of which is the first time used on American soil ever,” Curran said.

Officials acknowledged that the drone technology and its use by those with bad intent is rapidly changing. “Fiber-optic control drones now, dark drones. So it’s a constant chase to keep up with it,” Quinn said.

title: 14 years after woman was stabbed 100 times, her close friend was arrested
summary: Investigative genetic genealogy helped identify Mayra Velasquez, 42, as the suspect in Irasema Chavez’s 2012 stabbing death in the Arlington cold case.
story: For 14 years, the brutal killing of Irasema Chavez, who was stabbed more than 100 times in her Texas apartment in 2012, has remained a mystery.
Subscribe to read this story ad-free
Get unlimited access to ad-free articles and exclusive content.

After years of investigation and holding on to hope, authorities identified the suspect as Mayra Velasquez, 42, a friend of Chavez’s, the Arlington Police Department and the FBI announced at a news conference Wednesday.
Velasquez was arrested Thursday on a warrant charging her with capital murder. A motive in the stabbing remains unclear, police said.

Authorities said a suspect was identified through investigative genetic genealogy, a process that uses unidentified crime scene DNA, genealogical research and historical records to identify unknown DNA.
Chavez, 32, was found in her apartment, unresponsive and covered in blood, on Jan. 20, 2012.
She was declared dead at the scene, police said. The Tarrant County Medical Examiner’s Office determined she had been stabbed more than 100 times, police said.
Missing from her apartment was a TV, which investigators believed the suspect took.

Investigators collected a droplet of fresh blood on the bedroom television stand. The sample was sent to a crime lab for DNA analysis and was determined not to belong to Chavez but to an unknown Hispanic female.
The DNA profile was uploaded into the FBI’s Combined DNA Index System, a national database to compare DNA profiles in criminal investigations, but there was no match.
In November 2024, the Arlington police homicide unit met with the FBI Dallas field office about using investigative genetic genealogy to crack the case.
In April, the FBI’s investigative genetic genealogy team identified a potential suspect — Velasquez.
“Ms. Velasquez was at one time a close friend of Ms. Chavez and lived just a few miles away from the crime scene,” police said in a news release.
Velasquez had been in Chavez’s apartment before, Arlington Police Detective Tracey Dixon told reporters.
Dixon said Chavez’s cellphone has been a “valuable source of information about their relationship” but declined to go into further detail.

The following month, detectives obtained a sample of Velasquez’s DNA from discarded trash, sent it to a crime lab for further analysis and found it was a match to the blood droplet from Chavez’s murder scene.

Velasquez was arrested in the nearby city of Hurst and eventually transferred to the Tarrant County Jail, where she is being held without bond, according to online booking records. It’s not immediately clear whether she has an attorney.
Velasquez has an active sales agent license in the state, according to Texas Real Estate Commission records. No one answered at a number listed for a real estate company believed to be her employer.
For the family, the news was a sigh of relief after so many agonizing years.
“Being able to share that with the family is why we do this work,” Dixon said, tearing up. “They were very grateful. It was emotional.”

Joe Rothrock, the special agent in charge of the FBI Dallas field office, praised investigative genetic genealogy as “one of the most valuable tools law enforcement has today.” Since 2018, the FBI has used it to solve more than 250 cases across 30 states, he said.

title: The best ways to avoid (and treat) heat rash and sun poisoning, according to derms

But sometimes, a regular application of sunblock on your face and body isn’t enough. Outside of treating a sunburn, it’s important to be able to recognize, treat and avoid other conditions, like heat rash and even sun poisoning.

To find the best methods and treatments for heat rash and to learn how to actually know when a sunburn is actually sun poisoning, I spoke with dermatologists for their guidance and product recommendations. Plus, I also asked them about how to identify and treat these conditions in kids, too.

What is heat rash and how is it different from a sunburn?

Heat rash is a condition that dermatologists refer to as miliaria (not to be confused with malaria, the infectious disease carried by mosquitoes). It’s a form of inflammation on the skin that happens when sweat ducts become blocked and trapped under the skin’s surface, according to Caren Campbell, a board-certified dermatologist based in San Francisco.

“It typically shows up as small red bumps or clear blisters on the neck, chest, arms, or in skin folds like the groin and underarms, often with an itchy or prickly sensation,” she says. “Prolonged sweating in hot, humid conditions is the main driver, and tight or occlusive clothing makes it worse by trapping moisture against the skin.”
Heat rash is entirely different from a sunburn, which is a form of damage to skin cells caused by UV radiation, and heat rash can happen both in and outside of sunlight, according to Campbell.
How to treat and prevent heat rash
Wearing sunscreen is a must when you’re in the sun, but heat rash has more to do with sweat and being hot, so there are a few things Campbell says you should focus on:
Stay cool, dry and sweat free. Use a handheld fan to help dry sweat quickly.
Stay cool, dry and sweat free. Use a handheld fan to help dry sweat quickly.

Wear breathable clothing that keeps you cool and prevents sweating, and stay out of heat and sun for long periods of time. Consider investing in sweat-wicking tops, socks and more. It’s important to keep your skin as dry as possible, according to Campbell. Additionally, consider wearing UPF hats and UPF swimwear and clothing to protect your skin. Avoid heavy creams on your face and body, like emollients because they can clog your sweat ducts. If you develop a rash, “a gentle antibacterial cleanser can help, since bacteria on the skin surface may contribute to plugging the ducts,” says Campbell. Additionally, you can try applying a topical hydrocortisone if the rash is itchy.

How to treat and prevent heat rash in infants and children

Heat rash is often common in infants and toddlers since they have more sensitive skin than adults, and usually appears as small red bumps on the skin, according to Jennifer Mancuso, a pediatric dermatologist at the University of Michigan. As Campbell noted above, the best way to help infants and children avoid getting heat rash is to put them in breathable clothing that keeps them cool and sweat free.

Sometimes, this is particularly a challenge with infants and children if they’re prone to getting fevers, according to Mancuso. If they develop a heat rash that is itchy, Mancuso recommends using a topical cortisone or over-the-counter sensitive-skin moisturizer that’s fragrance free, according to Campbell.
What is sun poisoning and how is it different from a sunburn?
While sun poisoning isn’t technically a recognized medical term, it is typically just a very severe sunburn with several additional symptoms.

“A typical sunburn is red, tender, warm skin confined to the exposed areas,” Campbell says. Sun poisoning also often includes symptoms like fever, chills, blistering, nausea, dizziness and feeling dehydrated.
How to treat and prevent sun poisoning and sunburns
To prevent sun poisoning, you should stick with the following guidelines from our experts:

Be sure to wear sunscreen that has an SPF of 30 or greater and apply it every two hours, according to Campbell. Try to avoid the sun between 10 AM and 2 PM, when it’s strongest. Staying safe in the sun includes staying hydrated with electrolyte packets, using an antiperspirant to avoid sweat (which is a form water loss) and keeping a handheld fan handy, which many NBC Selected staff members do.

title: How to watch the 2026 MLS season
summary: This is everything you need to know about watching the 2026 MLS season, including streaming options and info on when the season takes place.
story: The World Cup may be over, but there are still plenty of ways you can get your soccer fix. The Major League Soccer season is currently up and running, where you can watch teams from across the US compete for the top spot.
To help you keep up with the matches, I’ve broken down everything you need to know about the MLS season, including when it runs and where you can stream.
When is the 2026 MLS season?

The 2026 MLS regular season kicked off on February 21 and runs through November 7. The league went on a pause period for the FIFA World Cup on May 25 and resumed matches on July 16, with the MLS All-Star Game taking place on July 29. Each of the 30 teams in the league will play 34 games (17 home and 17 away), after which the Audi 2026 MLS Cup Playoffs lineup will be decided at the end of the regular season on November 7, also known as Decision Day.
You can check the MLS website for the full match schedule along with league standings, team stats and more.
How to watch the 2026 MLS season
Apple TV

Apple TV is the only streaming service to show the entire MLS season, including every game, along with tournaments like the Leagues Cup and the MLS Cup Playoffs. You can get a subscription for $12.99 a month after a 7-day free trial.
DirectTV MySports

DirectTV’s MySports package gives access to Fox One and FS1, which allows you to watch select MLS matches live. You’ll also be able to watch over 20 other sports broadcasting channels, including ESPN. It costs $50 for the first two months, after which it increases to $65 per month.
FuboTV

FuboTV also has a Sports plan, which you can get for $46 for the first month, after which the price goes up to $56 per month. The plan includes Fox One and FS1 live channels, and can be added onto an already-existing subscription for $5 a month. The plans also all include unlimited Cloud DVR space, so you can record any games you may have missed to watch later.

title: How often should you wash and change out your sheets? Experts explain
summary: I talked to laundry experts to learn how often you should change and wash your bedding and when it’s time to throw them out for a new set.
story: There are so many different options online and in stores when it comes to bedding — the variety of pillowcases, flat sheets and comforters available makes it hard to know what to choose. What’s less confusing though is knowing that no matter what, your sheets need to be cleaned regularly to avoid stains, odors and just overall damage. Knowing just how often you should wash your sheets and bedding is a little more obscure, plus, even if your bedding is technically clean, sometimes it may just be time to replace it.

To find out how often you should change out and wash your sheets and when it’s time to replace them with a new set altogether, I spoke with laundry experts for their guidance. Keep reading to learn what they say, including how the rules change for pet owners who share the bed with their fur babies.

How often should you wash your sheets?

In general, you should change and wash your sheets around once a week, though this can depend on what type of bedding you’re referring to, according to Salvador Villarreal, the owner of laundry services company VIP Cleaners & Laundry. For things like fitted and flat sheets, once a week is standard, but for pillowcases, Villarreal recommends every three to seven days. Additionally, you should wash duvet covers every two to four weeks and comforters or duvet inserts at least every three weeks.

If you have pets that sleep in your bed with you and/or are prone to allergies, you should be washing your bedding more often, according to Villarreal. Consider changing your sheets twice a week and cleaning your duvet covers and inserts every two weeks regularly and never stretching it to four. You can wash mattress protectors every one to two months overall.
How often should you replace your sheets?

While it may depend on the type of bedding and factors such as how often you’ve been washing them, you should replace your sheets every two to five years, according to Villarreal. If your sheets have stains that are hard to get rid of, the fabric is becoming thin, pilling, tears and has less elasticity, then it’s time to replace them, says Villarreal.

“Duvet covers generally last longer since they protect the comforter underneath, while fitted sheets wear out first due to constant friction,” he says. Out of all types of bedding, though, fitted sheets should be replaced most often because of the friction they’re in contact with, according to Kim Romine, a fabric care scientist at Tide.

How do you wash sheets and bedding?

Outside of washing your sheets regularly, it’s also important that you actually use the best techniques to keep them clean and in proper shape. It’s best to use warm water that is between 90 and 105 degrees Fahrenheit, to allow them to be cleaned thoroughly while also preventing them from becoming damaged, according to Villarreal.

Another tip is to avoid overloading the washing machine to make sure clothes have room to move around. “Skip excessive detergent, since residue leaves fabric feeling stiff,” he says. “Tumble dry on medium heat and remove [them from the dryer] promptly to cut down on wrinkles and extend fabric life.”
Below are some additional pieces of advice from laundry experts for changing, washing and maintaining sheets to help them last before having to replace them.

It’s best to wash your sheets and bedding separately from other items, including towels, as this allows for more thorough cleaning and rinsing during the cycle, according to Romine. “Bedding specifically can accumulate sweat, body oils, skin cells, and personal care products over time. Washing these items separately can help ensure you aren’t overloading the wash with too much soil,” says Romine.  “You also want to make sure you aren’t overstuffing the load with fabrics so they have enough room to move freely in the wash, allowing detergent and water to more effectively remove soils.”When it comes to bedding, watch out for things like fraying on edges and seams, as this is a sign that, rather than washing, you should simply throw out and replace the sheet, according to Romine. title: Rep. Jim Jordan formally asks DOJ to prosecute Jack Smith over congressional testimony
summary: Jordan, chair of the House Judiciary Committee, accused Smith of lying in his testimony before the committee in December. Smith’s lawyers denied he made any false statements.
story: The top Republican on the House Judiciary Committee sent a letter to the Justice Department on Wednesday requesting a criminal investigation of former special counsel Jack Smith, alleging he made false statements during a congressional deposition last year.
Subscribe to read this story ad-free
Get unlimited access to ad-free articles and exclusive content.

Committee Chairman Jim Jordan, R-Ohio, wrote in a letter to acting Attorney General Todd Blanche that Smith “seemingly made willfully and intentionally false statements of material fact that contradict new documents” the Senate Judiciary Committee obtained this month.
Jordan asked the Justice Department to investigate Smith for a criminal charge, writing that his committee found “strong evidence” against him.
A spokesperson for the Justice Department confirmed receipt of the referral and said Wednesday that it “will investigate all evidence of criminal conduct.”
Smith has long been a target of President Donald Trump, who has disparaged him over his prosecutions of Trump.
Fox News first reported Jordan’s referral.

In a letter to Jordan and Blanche, attorneys for Smith denied that he made any false statements during his deposition, writing that he “provided truthful, responsive answers and candidly discussed his work as Special Counsel.”

“The referral is made not because Mr. Smith made a false statement — the letter concedes he did not — but because he did not proactively disclose information that was not responsive to a question asked,” lawyers Peter Koski and Lanny Breuer wrote.

The pair said the referral “reflects a chilling eagerness to weaponize the justice system by attacking a career, nonpartisan public servant who faithfully and fearlessly performed his duties by following the facts and the law.”

As special counsel, Smith oversaw two investigations beginning in 2022. One focused on election interference in the 2020 presidential election and the other on allegations that Trump mishandled classified documents after his first term ended. Trump denied any wrongdoing in both cases, which were dismissed in 2024 after he was elected to a second term. Longstanding DOJ policy prevents a sitting president from being prosecuted.
Jordan cited an exchange from Smith’s deposition before the committee on Dec. 17, when Smith was asked whether he sought a “search warrant for the content of any text messages from Members.”
Smith responded, “No, I don’t recall that.”
Asked whether he had asked only for toll records of the members of Congress, Smith said, “Correct.”

Rep. Jamie Raskin, D-Md., the ranking member of the committee, said in a statement Wednesday that Jordan’s referral “deliberately distorts and misstates the facts, including what questions the Republicans actually asked at Mr. Smith’s interview.”
“Congressional Republicans never asked Jack Smith about presidential records,” Raskin said.

Raskin argued that committee Republicans did not ask whether the messages from lawmakers were found on White House officials’ phones, whether the presidential records Smith subpoenaed included the messages or whether Smith’s team had ever “reviewed text messages from Members.”
“Jack Smith could not have lied because Republican Members never even asked the question their theory is based on,” he said.

Senate Republicans said last week that they had obtained documents from the Justice Department revealing Smith and his team reviewed text messages sent by 44 members of Congress as part of their investigations into Trump.

The documents the Senate Judiciary Committee obtained show that the messages were sent by lawmakers on both sides of the aisle, but mostly Republicans, to White House officials during Trump’s first term.

Smith’s team received the text messages from the National Archives and Records Administration in August 2023. They included text messages from October 2020 through Jan. 21, 2021, the committee said on July 14.

The Senate Judiciary Committee argued that because Smith’s team had not waited for a “Filter Team” to evaluate and segregate “privileged information” out of those messages, Smith and his team violated protections ensured by the Constitution’s Speech and Debate Clause.

“Smith’s team ran roughshod over the Constitution even after repeated warnings,” committee Chairman Chuck Grassley, R-Iowa, said in a statement on July 14. “Jack Smith has answering to do, and I intend to have him before the Senate Judiciary Committee in the coming months to hold him accountable.”
Grassley was on the list of members whose messages were reviewed, along with Jordan, former House Speaker Kevin McCarthy, R-Calif., and longtime Sens. John Cornyn, R-Texas, and Rand Paul, R-Ky.

title: ‘Off the charts’: Secret Service describes rising threats to protectees
summary: Despite the heightened environment, the Secret Service says it’s confident in plans for the rescheduled White House Correspondents’ Association dinner.
story: WASHINGTON — The Secret Service has opened more than 10,000 investigations this year into threats against people it protects, a 40% rise over the same period last year, officials said Wednesday.
Subscribe to read this story ad-free
Get unlimited access to ad-free articles and exclusive content.
Director Sean Curran told reporters at a briefing that the volatile political climate has reached a new level that he has not seen in his 24-year career.
He said the threat numbers are “off the charts.”

Despite the heightened environment — President Donald Trump has been the target of at least three assassination attempts — Curran and other senior leaders at the agency tasked with protecting Trump and other high-profile politicians are confident in security plans ahead of the rescheduled White House Correspondents’ Association dinner this week.

In April, a gunman stormed a security checkpoint, fired on an officer and was subdued before he reached the ballroom in Washington where Trump, the first lady, Cabinet officials and more than 2,600 journalists and other guests were in attendance.
Friday’s event will be held at a different Washington hotel with a much smaller ballroom and fewer guests. Trump is expected to attend and speak.
Curran said law enforcement is prepared.
“We will always evaluate every site. And right now, we have an advance team there, and they will take back and they will set up a plan to set that site up for success,” he said.
Deputy Director Matthew Quinn said the agency does not see a shadow cast by the April incident.

“We’re not looking at this as a redo of a dinner,” he said. “We’re looking at this as a presidential site with Cabinet members and other protectees there, just like every site we do everywhere we go.”
Curran said the security perimeter at the Washington Hilton worked because the gunman was kept a significant distance from Trump.
“We’re talking almost 120 yards from magnetometers to podium. That’s over a football field,” he said.
Beyond planning for Friday’s high-profile event, officials provided new insights about another emerging threat: drones.

The foiled plot to attack the June UFC fights at the White House included use of drones, according to court documents. Officials said they are deploying new detection methods around the White House and when the president travels.
“We’re also moving these assets around with the president, some of which is the first time used on American soil ever,” Curran said.

Officials acknowledged that the drone technology and its use by those with bad intent is rapidly changing. “Fiber-optic control drones now, dark drones. So it’s a constant chase to keep up with it,” Quinn said.

title: Alexander Kolodin, who tried to overturn Arizona election results, wins GOP nod for secretary of state
summary: Kolodin will face Democratic incumbent Adrian Fontes after defeating former state Republican Party chair Gina Swoboda, NBC News projects.
story: Republican state Rep. Alexander Kolodin will face Arizona’s Democratic secretary of state, Adrian Fontes, in November’s general election, NBC News projects, after he won the GOP primary.
Subscribe to read this story ad-free
Get unlimited access to ad-free articles and exclusive content.
Kolodin won the Republican nomination over former state GOP chair Gina Swoboda.

Kolodin, who has frequently questioned the results of past elections in interviews, led several lawsuits to overturn the results of the 2020 and 2022 elections in Arizona, earning rebukes from judges and the state bar association. Kolodin is backed by the conservative nonprofit group Turning Point USA and several Arizona GOP members of Congress.

Now, he’s running to be the chief election officer in a battleground state during the 2028 presidential campaign. Part of the role of secretary of state in Arizona is overseeing state elections. The office’s duties include working to certify “voting devices, election results, candidates and measures to the ballot, as well as the results of statewide elections,” according to the secretary of state’s website.
In a joint PBS interview featuring the two candidates, Kolodin said Arizona voters are looking for more transparency and openness in their elections.
“They are not getting that from Adrian Fontes; they will get that from me,” Kolodin said.

“I think voters in this primary and across this state have serious concerns with the way their elections are being administered,” he said. Kolodin also said people in the state can never be confident in their elections without more observers at polling stations.

Fontes, who previously ran elections in Maricopa County, Arizona’s largest county, has been outspoken about President Donald Trump and allies’ efforts to cast doubt on election results in Arizona and elsewhere. He defeated a Trump-endorsed Republican opponent in 2022 and is seeking a second term.
