Austin says she “hates” the ending of the poem.
“The ending is super dark. The vengeance is a cycle that just ends up repeating, and the only way in the actual poem that you get it to end is gods end it, and they make a forgetting,” she says.
In comparison, she likes how Nolan wrapped it up. In the movie, Odysseus and his wife Penelope self-exile, leaving their son in charge of Ithaca.
More About 'The Odyssey':

Burns, Bleach, Blindness: John Leguizamo Details Hair and Makeup Routine Behind His ‘Horrific’ ‘Odyssey’ Transformation‘The Odyssey’ Ending Explained: What Happens Next to OdysseusMatt Damon and His ‘Odyssey’ Co-Stars Debate What the Film Is Really About‘The Odyssey’ Reviews: What Critics Said to Earn the Movie a 98% Rotten Tomatoes Score
Burns, Bleach, Blindness: John Leguizamo Details Hair and Makeup Routine Behind His ‘Horrific’ ‘Odyssey’ Transformation
‘The Odyssey’ Ending Explained: What Happens Next to Odysseus
Matt Damon and His ‘Odyssey’ Co-Stars Debate What the Film Is Really About
‘The Odyssey’ Reviews: What Critics Said to Earn the Movie a 98% Rotten Tomatoes Score
“I was like, sure, let them go off into the sunset together, self-exile, prevent Telemachus from being tainted by the murder of everybody, like totally fine,” she says.
Christensen, meanwhile, found the ending to be a let down. For one, Damon’s Odysseus doesn’t kill all the suitors – he spares them. This merciful Odysseus felt unfamiliar to Christensen.

“What frustrates me is that it set him up to be merciful at the end. The men kneel down and he’s just like, ‘OK, I’m in exile now. Let’s go.’ Which, it’s just weird. What I wanted to happen, because it would have been more true to the poem, is for him to kill the kneeling men,” Christensen says.
He also likes the poem’s original ending for two reasons.
“It’s a complex political story about how we continue to live with people who’ve who’ve murdered our loved ones,” he says.
He also thinks it’s interesting that a poem about remembering ends with a mass forgetting: “It’s basically saying all of this is too dangerous.”
Odysseus’ act of mercy also underlines the difference in characterization between book and movie.

“Homer’s Odysseus is more realistic and complicated because it forces us to think about things aren’t black and white. Nolan’s Odysseus is more aspirational, which is ultimately more comforting because we all want the hero to be a good guy,” he says.
Zeus’ Law or the Golden Rule?
“The Odyssey” movie is hung up Zeus’ law, defined as the idea that anyone could be a god in disguise, so you must be welcoming. This is how the suitors get away with camping out at Ithaca for years.

But the trust and respect goes both ways. So, the Greek soldiers break with Zeus’ law when they hide inside the horse, meant to be a gift for the city, and sack Troy. Odysseus thinks this rupture has led to the breakdown of civilization.
Christensen says he thought it was “strange” that Zeus’ law came down to “do unto others and you would have them to unto you.”
“I guess it would be too hard to explain that you hospitality in the ancient world isn’t the same as like the Christian ideal,” Christensen says.
Circe — and Samantha Morton — Was the Highlight
Of all of Odysseus’ adventures, one stood out to the classicists.
“The scene that shows the promise of remaking Greek myth in film the most was the Circe scene,” Christensen says.

On their way home, Odysseus and his men visit Circe’s (Samantha Morton) island, where she lives alone — save for a few exotic animals. Turns out those animals, like lions and deer, are men whom she has transformed. Odysseus’ men are next.
After ravenously eating her stew, Odysseus’ men start to transform into pigs.

Morton’s turn as the character has been acclaimed. In a ranking of all of the performances in “The Odyssey,” Variety placed Morton at No. 1. She adds something new to the role, implying that she’s a victim of sexual assault in the past. “You’re giving her some motivation for her activity but it wasn’t too heavy,” Christensen says.
Austin, who went to see the movie in London with another classicist friend, said they were both “really grossed out” by the Circe scene, but loved it.
“We were having a lot of really similar reactions. We were a little bit vocal. I hope we did not annoy the people there, but we were really impressed,” she says.
Christensen also thought the siren scene was “really great.” Odysseus, in the movie, describes the song of the sirens as “the song of all the promises I failed to keep.”
“I found that type of internal deliberation and rumination really interesting,” Christensen says.

He adds that “most of the action scenes were just really well done. The sacking of Troy, the Trojan horse was imaginative. I think really effective. So those things really, really worked for me,” he says.

title: Colson Whitehead Says He Doesn’t Write Every Day: ‘Real Imposition on My Lifestyle, Frankly’
summary: Two-time Pulitzer winner Colson Whitehead opens up about his writing process and his new novel “Cool Machine” on “Glass Half Full.”
story: One of the core pieces of creative writing advice is rebuffed by bestselling novelist and two-time Pulitzer winner Colson Whitehead.
“People say, ‘Write every day.’ That seems like a real imposition on my lifestyle, frankly,” Whitehead told Craig Melvin for the July 21 episode of “Glass Half Full.”
“Sometimes I’m not feeling it. Sometimes it’s like, Thanksgiving, and you have to be present for your family or whatever. So that’s a lost week,” he said as Craig laughed.
Instead, Whitehead described his goal as hitting a certain number of pages a week.

“If I can do like six pages a week: Monday, Tuesday, Saturday and Sunday. That’s an accumulation. After a month you have like 20 something (pages), and after 10 months, you got, you know, 240,” he said.
Whitehead added that he feels “lucky” to work from home, where his writing routine can be a little more flexible — and unconventional.
“I can write a page, take a nap, do some spontaneous weeping, get back to work,” he said.
“That’s quite the process,” Craig said, before asking about Whitehead’s hobbies outside of work.

“When I’m not working, I’m really not working at all,” Whitehead said. “I cook a lot. I have a smoker, so a big slab of ribs, a brisket, that’s always fun in the summer. I’ll goof off and play video games. Stare off into space. Think about my regrets. And then when I’m ready to work, I’ll go back to work.”
He added that this hobbies inspire his work and help “clear my head” for what’s next.
Whitehead’s latest project, “Cool Machine,” hit shelves July 21. It’s the final volume in his “Harlem Trilogy,” which also contains bestsellers “Harlem Shuffle” and “Crook Manifesto.”
Although Whitehead told Craig that his newest book is always his favorite, “Cool Machine” still stands apart. The novel feels “closest” to who he is, he said.
“I really think I did what I set out to do,” Whitehead said. “I’m pretty proud of it.”
As for what’s next?
“My next work — my next book is enough of a stretch and a challenge,” Whitehead said.

“It’s a novel. It takes place in the 19-teens, and it’s not something I’ve done before. So the challenge of, ‘What am I doing? Why did I take this on?’ is exciting,” he added. “The characters are coming together.”

title: Robert Irwin Gets Emotional Helping Grieving ‘DWTS: The Next Pro’ Contestant After Mother’s Death
summary: Robert Irwin shared a special moment with a contestant during the latest episode of “Dancing With the Stars: The Next Pro” when the two bonded over losing one of their parents at a young age.
story: Robert Irwin shared a special moment with a contestant during the latest episode of “Dancing With the Stars: The Next Pro” when the two bonded over losing one of their parents at a young age.

In the second episode of the “Dancing With the Stars” spinoff, which aired July 20, the 14 remaining contestants were paired up and tasked with choreographing a dance that told the story of a significant moment in their lives. Dancer Allen Genkin, 36, decided to portray the absence he has felt since his mother died.

Genkin practiced the choreography with partner Adele Zaikman, explaining to her that for one particular move he wanted her to represent his mother being an angel looking over him. After rehearsals, Genkin became emotional and confided in Irwin, whose father Steve Irwin died when he was just 2 years old, and the two had a poignant conversation about grief.

“I wanted to visit Allen today because I know he’s telling a very important story, and a story that’s hard to tell. I want to see if I can help him through,” Robert Irwin, who hosts the competition series, explained in a voiceover.
While speaking with Genkin about the challenge, Robert Irwin said, “This week is heavy. But I feel like, particularly for you, it’s an important story.”
Genkin then shared that his mother, whom he described as his “best friend,” died when he was 15.

“You know, 20 years have gone by. They say time heals all wounds, but it really doesn’t,” he told Robert Irwin, who shook his head and agreed with Genkin. “And the only way I could really do it justice is to really showcase it through art, and that’s what I want to do.”
Robert Irwin said he could relate to Genkin because he also confronted the pain of losing a parent through dance.

“I understand what it’s like to lose someone. When I did ‘Dancing With the Stars,’ I was given this opportunity to do a dedication dance to my mom. As soon as that music stopped, my mom joined me on stage, and I completely broke down,” he recalled, referring to the Season 34 “Dedication Night” episode and the emotional embrace he shared with mom Terri Irwin.

Robert Irwin, who also performed a tribute to older sister Bindi Irwin in another episode and went on to win the season, continued, “It’s like you’re facing something for the first time in your life that you’ve never had the strength to face. But movement and dance, that is the thing that gives you the ability to face that.”
Genkin took the advice to heart and said he would use the dance as a chance to reconnect with his late mother.
“I think this is going to be the closest I’ve been to her since,” he said.
Tears filled Genkin and Robert Irwin’s eyes before the two hugged. “I’ll be right there with you, man,” Robert Irwin sweetly told him.
The 22-year-old zookeeper and conservationist has opened up before about grieving his dad, who died in September 2006 after a stingray attack.
During an interview on CNN’s “All There Is with Anderson Cooper” podcast in March, Robert Irwin revealed he still talks to his dad and feels his presence.

“I’m always closest to dad when I’m in the middle of nowhere, you know, when I’m out in the bush,” he shared. “There are absolutely moments where I’ll be hit with this sense of — it’s warmth, it’s like something kind of wraps around me.”
In those moments, he often asks his dad, “How do I go forward?”
Although he doesn’t hear an answer, he said he feels a “resolution.”

“There are these checkpoints that I find throughout life where you’re kind of going through the motions and then sometimes something will just hit you, and you need to just step away,” he said. “You need to download and you need to let loose. You need to go, ‘OK, I need to refocus on what is my grief journey.”

title: Lionel Messi Speaks Out After Argentina Loses World Cup: ‘The Pain Is Immense’
summary: Lionel Messi reflected on his 2026 World Cup journey, including Argentina’s wins and loss against Spain.
story: After a heartbreaking loss against Spain during the World Cup final, Lionel Messi is forever grateful for how far he and Team Argentina made it.
On July 19, Spain beat the reigning champs 1-0 in extra time, ending an incredible and historic World Cup run for the 39-year-old soccer legend.
Reflecting on the painful defeat in a July 20 Instagram post, Messi shared a photo of himself wearing his second place medal while on the pitch.
“El dolor es muy grande y va a costar que cierre esta herida,” he wrote in Spanish, which translates to, “The pain is immense and this wound will take time to heal.”

“But I will also hold onto all the good memories... The matches where we turned it around and gave it our all, moments that will remain in our memories forever, the support from our entire country which, with this group’s hard work and effort, brought us back among the best in the world,” he continued.
The one-time World Cup champ did note that right now, at this moment, “It is hard to fully appreciate” all that he and the team accomplished during the tournament.

“But this group reached two consecutive World Cup finals,” he wrote. “Thank you from the bottom of my heart for every greeting and every message. Once again, we managed to unite as a country and be together, sharing the immense pride of being Argentinian.”
He concluded his post by taking a moment to send a message to the new World Cup champs.
“I also want to congratulate Spain on winning the championship,” he wrote.
His comments section was filled with fans and brands thanking him for everything he’s contributed to the sport and his country. Many also called him the greatest of all time.

While this may be Messi’s final World Cup, the soccer star has participated in a total of six. He is, however, not retiring. The forward is currently a captain for Major League Soccer club Inter Miami. In 2025, he signed a contract with the team that extends through the 2028 MLS season.
The eight-time Ballon d’Or winner will have a short break as Inter Miami’s next match is July 22. Though, at this time, there is no confirmation if he will be playing in the game.

title: Does ‘The Odyssey’ Have an End Credits Scene?
summary: Does The Odyssey have an end credits scene? Here’s what to know about the ending of The Odyssey and what happens next.
story: Warning: This contains spoilers for the end of “The Odyssey.”
For nearly three hours, “The Odyssey” takes theatergoers on an epic journey.

The highly anticipated film was a hit at the box office in its first weekend of release, with the tale of Odysseus (Matt Damon) from one of the most celebrated works of literature in world history captivating movie fans to the tune of $264.1 million in ticket sales worldwide.

Packed with Hollywood stars like Damon, Anne Hathaway, Zendaya, Tom Holland, Lupita Nyong’o, Charlize Theron and Robert Pattinson, the movie has brought director Christopher Nolan’s vision of the ancient Greek epic to life and debuted to rave reviews.
“For me to take on Greek mythology on a big modern cinematic canvas is something that hasn’t been done,” Nolan told Kaylee Hartung on TODAY July 17.

A staple of many modern blockbusters has been an extra post-credits scene rewarding moviegoers who stick around until the absolute end. They have become a fixture in superhero and animated movies, popping up in “Masters of the Universe,” “Superman,” “The Fantastic Four: First Steps” and “Moana 2” among recent big films.
But when the credits roll on the nearly three-hour long “Odyssey,” is there one more scene at the end? Here’s what to know.
Is There a Post-Credits Scene at the End of ‘The Odyssey’?

No, once the swords-and-sandals epic has wrapped up after its 172-minute run time, that’s the end. There’s no secret scenes of Odysseus (Matt Damon) and his wife Penelope (Anne Hathaway) starting a new life in Los Angeles or anything.
Director Christopher Nolan had certainly done enough without needing any extra scenes, considering “The Odyssey” took three painstaking months to shoot all on 70-millimeter IMAX film.

“I definitely hit the limits of my own stamina and everybody’s stamina, I think. I mean, it’s ‘The Odyssey,’ of course it should be difficult,” he said on TODAY. “We’re not doing the job right making a film of ‘The Odyssey’ if it doesn’t seem difficult.”
So What Does Happen at the End of ‘The Odyssey’?
You would think there doesn’t need to be a spoiler alert for a story that was composed more than 2,000 years ago, but Nolan did put his own twist on the ending that differs from Homer’s epic poem.

In Nolan’s version, Odysseus and Penelope leave their son Telemachus (Tom Holland) behind and sail west toward the setting sun (probably not to Los Angeles). Odysseus is exiled, but he is with his beloved wife, who dreamed they would sail off together when news of the Trojan War first broke out.

In Homer’s version, the gods have much more of a say in how the story ends. Odysseus and Telemachus are about to battle all the angry families of Penelope’s suitors in Ithaca after Odysseus murdered all the wannabe husbands. However, the gods intervene.
“Zeus hurls a thunderbolt, and Athena makes them swear a truce,” Celsiana Warwick, assistant professor in the University of Iowa Department of Classics, tells TODAY.com.
Odysseus also isn’t done appeasing the gods, as the seer Tiresias tells Odysseus earlier in the poem that he must make a sacrifice to Poseidon in order to lift Poseidon’s curse on him.

title: ‘The Odyssey’ Ending Explained: Christopher Nolan’s Movie Rewrites the Poem in This 1 Way
summary: What happens at the end of the Odyssey? What happens next for Odysseus? This is Christopher Nolan’s twist and what the myth says.
story: Warning: This contains spoilers for the end of “The Odyssey.”
You might have read “The Odyssey” before, but Christopher Nolan’s rendering of the epic poem, part of the Homeric cycle, offers up a brand new experience.

That’s especially true of the ending. Nolan reimagines what happens when Odysseus, played by Matt Damon, returns to Ithaca after 10 years fighting in the Trojan War and another 10 years trying to return to his kingdom.
Here’s what to know about Nolan’s twist on the ending of “The Odyssey,” how the real poem ends and the surprising, and unofficial, continuation of Odysseus’ story.
What Happens at the End of Christopher Nolan’s ‘The Odyssey’?
Nolan’s “Odyssey” will be unfamiliar for those who read the epic poem.
It’s a bittersweet ending for Odysseus and his wife, Penelope (Anne Hathaway). After murdering the suitors who had been trying to court her, Odysseus is exiled from Ithaca.

He and Penelope leave their son Telemachus (Tom Holland) behind and sail west toward the setting sun, which is what Penelope dreamed they’d do when news of the Trojan War first broke out. Yes, he’s exiled — but at least they’re together.

Odysseus also reckons with the dire outlook for civilization at large and his role in it. Odysseus feels that the invasion of Troy broke “Zeus’ law,” cited throughout the movie — the code of conduct that says you should treat hosts and guests well, because anyone could be a god. The Trojan Horse, an act of war disguised as a gift, was a breach of the code.

Odysseus feels that this has led to the collapse of civilization. The “sea people,” spoken of throughout the movie with fear, are the returning Greek soldiers sacking towns, and spreading the violence that started in Troy.
He references the idea of oral history, which is how “The Odyssey” and its companion story “The Iliad” began. When people can no longer read, they will tell the stories of Troy in poems.

Scholar Joel Christensen, editor of “The Oxford Critical Guide to Homer’s Odyssey,” points out that Damon’s Odysseus does something Homer’s Odysseus doesn’t: Spares some of the suitors’ lives. He says Damon’s Odysseus is more of a “good guy” than the original.
“What I wanted to happen because it would have been more true to the poem is for him to kill the kneeling men,” Christensen says.
What Happens at the End of Homer’s ‘The Odyssey’?
“The ending of ‘The Odyssey’ is kind of strange,” Celsiana Warwick, assistant professor in the University of Iowa Department of Classics, tells TODAY.com.
The Hollywood version of the story might end with Penelope and Odysseus’ reunion. But that would have been “unsatisfying” to an ancient audience, Warwick says.

Instead, Odysseus has to face consequences for murdering all of the suitors, which compromise an elite swath of Ancient Greece’s population. The families of the suitors swarm Ithaca, wanting to get revenge on Odysseus and Telemachus. They’re about to rush into battle when the gods intervene. “Zeus hurls a thunderbolt, and Athena makes them swear a truce,” Warwick says.
Warwick adds that the ending speaks to an element of Greek culture during the archaic period “where blood feuds between aristocratic families could get way out of hand.”
“That’s something that would have been of great interest to an ancient audience, perhaps not so much to a modern audience,” she says.

Odysseus’ wandering continues, too, though his departure from Ithaca is not actually depicted in “The Odyssey.” Earlier on in the poem, the seer Tiresias tells Odysseus what he must do after killing the suitors.

In order to lift Poseidon’s curse, Odyssey has to take an oar and go on a journey until he finds men who don’t recognize it and know nothing of the sea. There, he will make a sacrifice to Poseidon, and all will be well. Tiresias predicted he would die of old age.
Jonathan Burgess, Emeritus professor of Classics, University of Toronto, calls the poem’s ending a “happy” one.

“There’s the recognition that things will follow. Poseidon’s still mad, but in the underworld, Odysseus was told how to stop Poseidon from being angry at him. There’s another adventure coming, but it’s a solution to anger from the divinity Poseidon — something you don’t want to hang over your life,” he says.
What Happens to Odysseus After ‘The Odyssey’?

“The Odyssey” ends with the gods intervening in a suitors’ battle. However, there’s more about Odysseus to be found in “other epics about the Trojan War and what happens after the Trojan War,” Burgess says.

“These existed apparently around the same time as ‘The Iliad’ and ‘The Odyssey.’ Same meter, same kind of poetry, same tradition. They told the whole story, starting from Paris and Helen to the sack of Troy,” Burgess says.
Unlike “The Iliad” and “The Odyssey,” these poems don’t exist in full. Instead, only fragments survived. Proclus, a Roman grammarian, wrote down summaries.
“The cycle poems were valued as context for Homer, but the poems themselves were not valued enough to be sung or to be preserved by the Roman period,” Burgess says.

The epic cycle concludes with “The Telegony,” which is about what happened after Odysseus’ homecoming. Author Madeline Miller looked to “The Telegony” for her popular book “Circe,” about the witch who hosts Odysseus during “The Odyssey.”
“The Telegony” is about Telegonus, the son Odysseus had during his time with Circe. Telegonus is not mentioned in “The Odyssey.”
He goes out in search of his father, carrying weapons from his mom — one being a poison-tipped spear. Eventually, he uses that spear on his father.
“Telegonus has never seen Odysseus. Odysseus has never seen Telegonus. Odysseus assumes he’s some stranger trying to steal his cattle. So they fight, and Telegonus kills his dad,” Burgess says.
Then comes something, perhaps, even stranger. First, Telegonus and Telemachus bring the corpse of Odysseus back to Aeaea, the island of Circe, and bury the body.
“Some people say Circe married Telemachus, and that Telegonus married Penelope. So there’s this strange two new weddings at the end of ‘The Telegony,’” Burgess says.

Burgess says Odysseus also remarries, according to certain myths. After leaving Ithaca to make a sacrifice for Poseidon, he travels to Epirus in northwest Greece. He married Callidice and has a son, Polypoetes, Burgess shares. After Callidice dies, he returns to Ithaca — setting the scene for “The Telegony.”
“The Telegony” place in relation to “The Odyssey” remains a mystery.
“Clearly, ‘The Telegony’ knows of ‘The Odyssey,’ but does ‘The Odyssey’ know of ‘The Telegony’”? Warwick asks.
She thinks “The Telegony” might speak to the idea of tying up loose ends.
“I think it is meant to be a happy ending. This is a way for his family to be happy without him,” Warwick says.

title: Marcello Hernández Goes Off-Script on TODAY, Leaving Al and Sheinelle in Shambles
summary: Marcello Hernández’s impression of Kevin Hart on TODAY left Sheinelle Jones and Al Roker in tears from laughing so much.
story: Hernández plus Hart equals hilarity.

Marcello Hernández and Kevin Hart, who star in the upcoming Netflix comedy “72 Hours,” stopped by TODAY July 20 for an interview that went off the rails when the “Saturday Night Live” star did an impression of the veteran comedian.
Things were already a bit goofy when Sheinelle Jones asked Hernández what it was like working with Hart.
“Do you want to see it? Should I show you?” he replied. “This is what it’s like to work with Kevin Hart.”
Hernández then launched into an impression of Hart on set, telling Sheinelle to pretend to be him asking Hart for advice.
“I’m sorry,” Hernández, fully in character as Hart, said, cutting her off while acting like he was on a phone call.

“They gotta bring the money up!” he said. “Money’s gotta be up if you want me to do that. Listen, I’m good. I’m good, but it’s gonna cost ya! I’m good. I know what I’m doing. Yeah, I’ll be there ... for a price!”
Sheinelle and Hart doubled over in laughter, while the TODAY crew could be heard cackling in the background.
“Add a zero!” Hernández said.
“This is ridiculous,” Hart said in response to the impression.
“No, it’s not,” Hernández fired back, while pointing out that Hart had AirPods behind him.
He joked Hart had the earbuds “just in case a CEO calls and is like, ‘We want Kevin to be the face of Froot Loops.’”
Sheinelle continued to howl, while the camera cut away to Al Roker, who was also doubling over in laughter.
Hernández finally broke character and gushed about Hart.
“I’m grateful to work with Kevin,” he said. “He’s a nice guy.”
Hart returned the kind words.
“I got to witness this in real time. But he is exactly what you would think that he is,” he said, adding that his co-star did “an amazing job” hosting the 2026 ESPY Awards.
Hernández wasn’t quite finished poking fun at Hart, teasing him about his shirt.

“Kevin is waking up in the morning going, ‘Which shirt should I wear? Should I wear a normal shirt, like a human being, or should I put on this weird rust-silver combo? Looks like I’m golfing, but also I’m the maître d’ at a steakhouse,’” he joked.
“Why don’t you ever wear socks? How about we talk about that?” Hart fired back.
“Because I’m Dominican,” Hernández said.
The whole interaction was just too much for Sheinelle.
“I can’t, I can’t,” she said as the interview drew to a close. “I don’t even need to say anything else.”
She then tossed to Al for the weather.
“Add another zero to the temperature,” Al joked, drawing laughs.

title: How to Watch the World Cup Final, Including Closing Ceremony and Halftime Show
summary: The 2026 FIFA World Cup final takes place July 19 between TEAM and TEAM. It will include a star studded closing ceremony and halftime show.
story: The 2026 FIFA World Cup championship takes place July 19 at the New York New Jersey Stadium, better known as MetLife Stadium, in East Rutherford, New Jersey.

The tournament’s final game between reigning champion Argentina and Spain will make history by featuring the first-ever FIFA World Cup Final Halftime Show, an 11-minute extravaganza co-headlined by pop superstars Justin Bieber, Madonna, Shakira and BTS, among others.
For the latest World Cup info, follow TODAY.com’s liveblog
A star-studded closing ceremony will celebrate the tournament’s 48 teams from around the world with performances by Post Malone, Nicole Scherzinger, Robbie Williams, Laura Pausini and IShowSpeed.
Tom Cruise will also make a special appearance during the closing ceremony. EGOT winner Jennifer Hudson will be on hand to perform the United States national anthem just ahead of the game.
Mexico, Canada and the U.S. hosted nearly 100 matches across venues in 16 cities, making the 2026 World Cup the biggest ever.
Read on to learn how to watch the 2026 FIFA World Cup final.
When Does the 2026 World Cup Closing Ceremony Start?

The 2026 World Cup’s closing ceremony now starts at 1:30 p.m. ET on July 19, ahead of the final championship match at New York New Jersey Stadium, also known as MetLife Stadium, in East Rutherford, New Jersey.
The closing ceremony will feature performances by Nicole Scherzinger, Robbie Williams, Laura Pausini and IShowSpeed.
Oscar winner Tom Cruise will also make a special appearance and EGOT winner Jennifer Hudson will sing the U.S. national anthem.
When Does the Match Start?
The 2026 World Cup’s final match kicks off at 3 p.m. ET.
Who Will Perform at the 2026 FIFA World Cup  Final Halftime Show?
This year’s World Cup features the tournament’s first-ever halftime show.
Justin Bieber, Madonna, Shakira and BTS will co-headline the 11-minute show.
Burna Boy, Gustavo Dudamel and PS22 Chorus featuring Coldplay are also set to perform.

Soccer fans in the U.S. can tune into the 2026 FIFA World Cup final live on FOX and in Spanish on Telemundo.
The tournament’s final can also be streamed live on Peacock, FOX Sports, YouTube TV and Fubo.

title: Xzibit Shares He Still Has The Same Beloved Cat From His ‘Pimp My Ride’ Days
summary: “Pimp My Ride” host Xzibit shared in a social media post on July 16 that Thunder Cat, a cat that he’s had since 2006, is still with him to this very day.
story: Be still our millennial hearts.
Rapper Xzibit shared in a social media post on July 16 that Thunder Cat, a pet that he’s had since 2006, is still with him to this very day.
As many a millennial has pointed out, that means that Xzibit has had his buddy with him since his days, hosting popular MTV show “Pimp My Ride,” which ran from 2004 to 2007.

People were more than impressed with Thunder Cat’s longevity. And with the show centered around turning banged up cars into impressive, often-outrageously upgraded rides, social media users couldn’t help but have a little fun.

“Yo dawg we heard you like cats so we put a litter box and a scratching post in your ‘03 Lincoln Navigator. We call it ‘Navigato’,” one Instagram user commented, mimicking Xzibit’s iconic lines on the show.
Others parodied the show’s theme song.
“🎶 So you wanna be a cool cat? But your kitty ain’t fly? You gotta hit me up because I’m a pretty cool guy ….It’s ya boy X to Z XZibit!” a social media user wrote.
And many others pointed out how Thunder Cat has lived through quite a bit, with one Instagram user writing, “Thunder Cat’s been judging people since MySpace.”

“Pimp My Ride” lasted for six seasons. It cemented the rapper as an iconic MTV television host as he helped hopelessly unskilled drivers turn their vehicles into “pimped out” masterpieces with the experts at auto repair shop West Coast Customs.
The modifications were often just plain wild, as Xzibit would surprise participants with add-ons like a mobile CAT scan machine, a slot machine and a snow cone machine.
Netflix attempted an eight-episode reboot of the show entitled “Resurrected Rides” in 2024. But it was hosted by “SNL” alum Chris Reed rather than Xzibit.
The rapper was so touched by the excitement over Thunder Cat from fans, he posted a follow-up photo on July 18 with the little lady.
“Yall made the last Thunder Cat post go viral,” Xzibit wrote on Instagram. “So she got a battery in her back acting like she ready to have her own s---… 🤦🏽‍♂️”

title: Burns, Bleach, Blindness: John Leguizamo Details Hair and Makeup Routine Behind His ‘Horrific’ ‘Odyssey’ Transformation
summary: Actor John Leguizamo reveals the bleach, the burns and the “severe emotional breakdowns” he underwent during the filming of the blockbuster movie “The Odyssey.”
story: When the camera cuts, the interview isn’t over. With “Cut for Time,” TODAY.com asks the burning questions our anchors couldn’t get to on-air.

If you look closely, you can spot John Leguizamo sporting a red track suit in the background of Madonna’s 1984 video, “Borderline.” It’s one of many under-fives the scrappy young comedian took along the way to Hollywood success.
A veteran of stage, film and television, Leguizamo’s resume is a  roundup of notable movies including “Moulin Rouge!” “Encanto” and “Ice Age,” as well as TV dramas like “ER” and “When They See Us.”

But it’s his latest role as Eumaeus, loyal servant to Odysseus (played by Matt Damon), in Christopher Nolan’s blockbuster “The Odyssey” that Leguizamo, who turns 66 on July 22, says is the “highlight of my life.”
Even so, the actor reveals that over the months he shot the film, he was bleached, burned and, at times, emotionally broken.

Charming and dangerously funny, Leguizamo sat down in TODAY’s Orange Room to unpack it all, including why he was afraid to be left alone on the set of “The Odyssey” and the reason he gave his canine co-star, Argus, an NSFW nickname.

title: Oil surges past $95 as U.S. downplays Iran diplomacy and 2nd trade route is disrupted
summary: The international benchmark Brent crude rose almost 5% to hit more than $95 per barrel for the first time in almost six weeks.
story: The price of oil surged nearly 5% Wednesday as U.S. officials talked down the chance of new peace talks after an 11th straight night of strikes on Iran and with major disruption now facing two of the world’s key supply routes.
Subscribe to read this story ad-free
Get unlimited access to ad-free articles and exclusive content.
International Brent crude oil rose as much as 4.9% to more than $95 per barrel for the first time in almost six weeks. U.S. crude oil rose as much as nearly 5.1% to nearly $89 per barrel.
Those prices pulled back slightly by the afternoon. U.S. crude closed higher by 2.9%, at $86.83 per barrel while Brent closed up 3.4%, at $94.07 per barrel.
While Brent is widely considered the international oil benchmark, it also influences the retail cost of gas in the U.S.

Those pump prices rose again Wednesday, extending their climb above $4 per gallon. The national average price rose 4 cents overnight to $4.06 per gallon, according to motor club AAA data tracked by NBC News.
Treasury yields spiked, following oil’s latest jump and its likely impact on inflation. As of midmorning trading, the U.S. 10-year Treasury yield was hovering around 4.65%, its highest since May.
As a result, the average rate on a 30-year mortgage rose to 6.75% Wednesday, matching its highest level of the year.

Since the start of the month, oil prices have gained 25% and are now up more than 50% since the start of the year. That move has largely erased the drop in prices that came after the U.S. and Iran signed a memorandum of understanding in mid-June.
Rhetoric escalates tensions
President Donald Trump had declared that tentative deal, which was aimed at ending the war and reopening the Strait of Hormuz, “over” on July 8.
But on Wednesday, Trump ratcheted up the rhetoric once again.

“Any time the Islamic Republic of Iran shoots at a ship in the Strait of Hormuz, whether it be by Missile, Rocket, Drone, or any other device or weapon, the United States will bomb and destroy ONE BRIDGE OR POWER PLANT, including those located next to, or in, the Capital City of Tehran,” he posted on social media.
Overnight, Secretary of State Marco Rubio said that the U.S. remained open to diplomacy with Iran, “but right now they don’t seem to be serious about that.”
Rubio added that the U.S. would continue to try to protect commercial shipping.

But in the last two days, the U.K.’s Maritime Trade Organization has reported multiple attacks on vessels in the area. In at least two of those, said the maritime monitoring group, which is aligned with the British navy, crews were forced to abandon ship.
Those attacks are one reason traffic in the Strait of Hormuz remains extremely low.
On Monday, only 13 ships crossed the vital waterway, and on Tuesday that number was only nine, according to an analysis of ship movements by MarineTraffic.

title: Trump attends dignified transfer of 4 service members killed in Iran attacks
summary: The president has attended two previous dignified transfers since the war began; this is the first since he declared the ceasefire over.
story: President Donald Trump on Wednesday attended the dignified transfer of the remains of four service members killed in Iranian attacks this month after hostilities ramped up following the collapse of the ceasefire.
Subscribe to read this story ad-free
Get unlimited access to ad-free articles and exclusive content.

The four service members being flown from the Middle East to Dover Air Force Base were 28-year-old Angel S. Rampersad of New York, 30-year-old Michael Emmanuel Swinton of North Carolina, 25-year-old Tyler James Feehan of Hawaii and 19-year-old Isabella Gonzales of Texas.

Dignified transfers are some of the most solemn occasions for presidents, who often attend to pay respects to troops killed in conflicts overseen by them as commander in chief. Trump has attended two prior dignified transfers since the war began in February, but this is his first since he declared on July 8 that the ceasefire was over.

The event marked the latest impact of the war, which has garnered criticism from lawmakers on both sides of the aisle who question the administration’s strategy in the monthslong conflict. The hostilities, which were paused after the two sides agreed to a peace plan that quickly fell apart, have thrown the region into chaos, leaving at least 18 Americans dead, costing at least $37.5 billion and inflating the price of oil.
The president and his administration have vigorously defended their handling of the war, arguing it is necessary to prevent Iran from acquiring a nuclear weapon.

Trump told reporters earlier Wednesday: “We’re going to Dover. Some of you are going with us. To honor our heroes, and they are indeed great heroes, actually. They said, and all of them said very strongly, we can’t let, we cannot let Iran have a nuclear weapon. They won’t have a nuclear weapon. So we’re going to honor them. And it’s one of the hardest things to do, for me, it’s one of the hardest things to do as a president, but has to be done.”

The family members of the fallen service members attended the dignified transfer, where the bodies of their loved ones were moved in American flag-draped transfer cases from a plane into waiting vans.

Uniformed service members marched the transfer cases past officials, including Trump, Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, Chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff Gen. Dan Caine and White House press secretary Karoline Leavitt. Sens. Thom Tillis, R-N.C., and Chris Coons, D-Del., also attended.
Trump and other officials saluted as the remains passed before them, while others placed their hands on their hearts. The president also met privately with the families, the White House confirmed.
Gonzales was killed Friday and Feehan was killed Saturday, the Pentagon said. It also said that Swinton was killed Sunday “during a controlled detonation” of an attack drone.

Rampersad was “believed to have been killed” in Jordan, the Pentagon said, adding that “the incident is under investigation.” The Pentagon has said that she is believed to have been the missing soldier who is presumed dead.
Add NBC News to Google
Add NBC News to Google
Hegseth faced questions from senators Tuesday about the cost and strategy of the war during a tense hearing on the Pentagon’s budget request.

During one particularly heated exchange, Sen. Gary Peters, D-Mich., called the Trump administration’s efforts “an utter and complete failure” and pressed Hegseth on what the long-term plan is to end the war.

“You have over a trillion dollars,” Peters said. “You’re asking for one and a half trillion dollars. It’s not a question of money. It’s a question of leadership and understanding what it takes to actually win.”

title: U.S. signs landmark nuclear agreement with Saudi Arabia
summary: The U.S. will support creating a civilian nuclear power program in the kingdom under the agreement, a senior administration official told NBC News.
story: The U.S. signed a landmark nuclear agreement with Saudi Arabia on Wednesday, the Energy Department announced on X.
Subscribe to read this story ad-free
Get unlimited access to ad-free articles and exclusive content.

“U.S. Secretary of Energy Chris Wright and Saudi Minister of Energy His Royal Highness (HRH) Prince Abdulaziz bin Salman signed a peaceful nuclear cooperation agreement, commonly known as a 123 agreement, alongside an accompanying bilateral safeguards agreement,” the announcement read. “Together, these two agreements lay the legal foundation for a decades-long, multi-billion-dollar partnership that advances several priority economic and strategic objectives, including nuclear nonproliferation.”

In the announcement, Wright added: “Rest assured, these agreements uphold the highest standards of nuclear safety and nonproliferation, while relying on the world’s best nuclear technology and scientists, designed right here in the United States.”
Earlier, a senior administration official told NBC News that President Donald Trump had approved the deal.

The U.S. will support creating a nuclear power program and American companies will build the program in the kingdom under the agreement, said the official, who was granted anonymity to speak about the deal before its official announcement.

The deal is not expected to require the most rigorous level of U.N. inspections or include a ban on uranium enrichment or reprocessing of spent nuclear fuel, according to three people familiar with the agreement.

The pact would allow U.S. companies to build a uranium enrichment facility in Saudi Arabia pending a joint U.S.-Saudi study examining whether such a step would be feasible, the people said. The text of the deal has not been released, and the administration has not publicly outlined its details.
The Wall Street Journal first reported news of the agreement.

Congress will be required to vote on the agreement but would need a veto-proof majority to actually block it, which could pave the way for the kingdom to pursue its own uranium enrichment and would be likely to raise fears of nuclear proliferation.

Asked ahead of the announcement about those concerns and reports of an expected deal, Secretary of State Marco Rubio said Wednesday that the U.S. would not “reach any agreement with any country in the world that leads to the risk of proliferation.”

The agreement comes as the war against Iran that the U.S. and Israel launched in late February goes on. Trump has insisted that Tehran should not be able to develop a nuclear weapon, even as the Islamic Republic consistently denies it plans to do so.

An agreement to normalize ties between Israel and Saudi Arabia had been a U.S. requirement for any deal allowing the kingdom to enrich uranium, but Saudi leaders insisted that would not be possible without meaningful progress toward a Palestinian state.

However, Wright discussed building the country’s commercial nuclear power industry with his Saudi counterpart, Prince Abdulaziz bin Salman Al Saud, on a visit to the kingdom last year, shortly before Trump traveled there himself in May 2025.

Any deal without appropriate guardrails would be “concerning from a proliferation perspective,” said Darya Dolzikova​, a senior research fellow with the proliferation and nuclear policy program at the Royal United Services Institute, a London-based think tank.
“Any country, period, but particularly countries of proliferation concern have to be really, really robust on their nonproliferation provisions,” she added.
And Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman has warned that the kingdom would try to obtain a nuclear weapon if Iran were also able to, Dolzikova​ noted.

Saudi Arabia also signed a mutual defense pact with Pakistan, the only Muslim nuclear nation, in September. Pakistani Defense Minister Khawaja Asif then said his country’s nuclear program would “be made available” to Saudi Arabia if required.

Saudi Arabia is a member state of the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA), which promotes peaceful nuclear work but also inspects nations to ensure they do not have clandestine atomic weapon programs. Based in Vienna, the agency reports to the United Nations General Assembly and Security Council.

While enrichment does not necessarily lead to a nuclear weapon, it can open the door to it. However, any country wishing to pursue one would also have to master other technologies, including the use of synchronized high explosives.

And there has been focus on whether any deal would include the “gold standard” safeguards that would block Saudi Arabia from enriching uranium and reprocessing spent nuclear fuel, both of which are potential pathways to nuclear weapons.
It also remains to be seen whether the agreement includes the “Additional Protocol” that grants the IAEA greater oversight of a country’s nuclear activities.

Ultimately, “the devil will be in the details,” said Sanam Vakil, director of the Middle East and North Africa program at the London-based think tank Chatham House. If Saudi Arabia does retain the right to enrich, she said, “it’s the issue of domestic enrichment that will be more concerning and alarming.”

The deal with the U.S. came a day after senior Saudi and United Arab Emirates officials shared similar social media posts ​affirming their close historical ties and “wise leadership,” a move that follows months of tensions owing to a rift ‌between the two Persian Gulf monarchies.

The Gulf nations have been divided over ​their support for opposing sides in the war in Yemen, which culminated in a Saudi airstrike late last year on what it said was a shipment of UAE military equipment to the Yemeni faction Abu Dhabi backed.
Their interests have diverged over a number of issues, including oil quotas.
But the posts from Saudi Media Minister Salman Al-Dosary and Abdulla bin Mohamed Alhamed, chairman of the UAE National Media Authority, said they should focus on their shared history and heritage.

title: U.S. military identifies soldiers killed in Iranian attack in Jordan
summary: The Pentagon identified the soldiers as 25-year-old Tyler James Feehan of Hawaii and 19-year-old Isabella Gonzales of Texas.
story: The Defense Department on Monday released the names of two soldiers killed in Iranian strikes in Jordan, identifying them as 25-year-old Tyler James Feehan of Hawaii and 19-year-old Isabella Gonzales of Texas.
Subscribe to read this story ad-free
Get unlimited access to ad-free articles and exclusive content.
Gonzales was killed Friday and Feehan on Saturday. The Pentagon did not provide details on the exact circumstances of their deaths.
Feehan and Gonzales had been assigned to Army missile defense commands in Fort Bragg, North Carolina, and Ansbach, Germany, respectively, it said.
The Pentagon said they were part of a longtime, ongoing mission to counter ISIS, Operation Inherent Resolve, that began in 2014.

The service members were not technically part of the war with Iran, dubbed Operation Epic Fury by the Pentagon, despite President Donald Trump saying Sunday that they were killed while ensuring Iran does not get a nuclear weapon.
“Those great patriots were out there fighting that Iran cannot have a nuclear weapon,” Trump told reporters.
In addition, another U.S. service member was killed in a separate incident in Iraq.

The release of the two soldiers’ identities comes after the U.S. military announced Sunday that it had recovered unidentified human remains while searching for an American service member reported missing following an Iranian missile and drone attack in Jordan.

U.S. Central Command said military personnel found the remains Sunday at the site of Friday’s attack in Jordan. Officials said an examination is underway to determine whether they belong to the missing service member.
On Tuesday, the Pentagon announced the “believed to be death of an active-duty Soldier who was supporting overseas operations in Jordan” in a statement.

“Sgt. Angel S. Rampersad, 28, of Ozone Park, New York, is believed to have been killed in action on July 17, 2026, during an enemy attack at Muwaffaq Salti Air Base, Jordan. The incident is under investigation. U.S. Central Command previously announced this Soldier as missing. The Soldier status was updated to a Duty Status–Whereabouts Unknown and is believed to be deceased,” the statement said.
Central Command said Saturday that two service members were killed and a third was missing following Iran’s attack Friday on U.S. and partner forces in Jordan.

Separately, a U.S. service member was killed Saturday in northern Iraq during the controlled detonation of unexploded ordnance from a downed Iranian one-way attack drone, the combatant command said. A second service member suffered a minor injury and remains under medical care.
“Our hearts go out to these families,” Secretary of State Marco Rubio told reporters Sunday. “These are heroes that pay the ultimate price.”

In a social media post Monday, Trump said U.S. military leaders had been given the directive to make Iran pay “many times over” for the killing of U.S. soldiers. White House press secretary Karoline Leavitt said Monday afternoon in a post on X that the president would attend the transfer of the remains of the service members at Dover Air Force Base in Delaware on Tuesday night.
Leavitt later posted on X that the transfer of remains would not take place Tuesday. “The exact day and time are still being finalized,” she wrote.

Fifteen U.S. service members have been killed in combat since military operations against Iran began, while two more service members died from noncombat-related causes. American military members who have been wounded since the start of the conflict now number 140, including eight who were wounded severely.
The discrepancy in the naming of the conflict reflects an ongoing confusion about the war with Iran — specifically about whether Operation Epic Fury continues.

NBC News previously reported that the Trump administration was considering renaming the start of combat operations in Iran to circumvent the 1973 War Powers Resolution, which requires troops to be withdrawn within 60 days of starting combat operations if Congress was not notified beforehand.
In May, Trump notified Congress that Operation Epic Fury had ended. Since then, the Pentagon has not said what the ongoing military operation in Iran is named.

The military says Operation Inherent Resolve is the Combined Joint Task Force that works with partner forces to ensure the defeat of the Islamic State militant group. Asked about the discrepancy in the mission the fallen service members were on, acting Pentagon press secretary Joel Valdez said in a statement, “They were deployed on orders to support Operation Inherent Resolve.”

There are more than 50,000 troops in the region, according to U.S. Central Command. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth and Chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff Gen. Dan Caine last gave a briefing at the Pentagon on the Iran war in May.
At least 3,375 people have been killed in Iran since military operations began, according to the country’s state-affiliated news media, citing a senior judicial official.

The mounting death toll has effectively ended the interim ceasefire between the U.S. and Iran negotiated last month. After weeks of trading accusations that each side has violated the agreement, the two countries resumed attacks, with U.S. forces striking Iranian military targets and Tehran launching missiles and drones at U.S. allies in the region.
Rubio said that the U.S. remained open to diplomacy with Iran, but that “even within their own system, there’s a growing split.”

“They continue to send signals that they want to talk, that they want to negotiate,” he said. “But their behavior is what we’re responding to, and their behavior is they’re launching missiles and drones against ships, including tonight.”
“Their behavior has to change in order for ours to change,” Rubio added.

On Sunday evening, Central Command said it conducted a ninth consecutive night of attacks on Iran starting at 7 p.m. ET. It said in a subsequent statement shortly after 10 p.m. ET that the strikes had concluded.

“CENTCOM assets targeted Iranian military command centers, air defense and coastal surveillance sites, maritime capabilities, missile and drone launch sites, and communications networks to further diminish Iran’s ability to attack commercial vessels and civilian mariners transiting the Strait of Hormuz,” it said.

On Saturday, the command said U.S. forces completed the eighth night of launching munitions against Iran when it targeted Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps forces believed to have been involved in Friday’s attack on U.S. service members in Jordan.

The military said the two service members died defending against an Iranian ballistic missile and drone attack. Four other U.S. service members were medically evacuated to hospitals in Jordan and have since been discharged.

title: Ukraine’s Zelenskyy fires his commander in chief after protests and major rift
summary: The firing caps a crisis for Volodymyr Zelenskyy after Ukrainians took to the streets to call for Oleksandr Syrskyi’s resignation.
story: Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy fired his commander in chief, Oleksandr Syrskyi, on Tuesday, bowing to pressure after the removal of popular Defense Minister Mykhailo Fedorov sparked the fiercest leadership crisis of his presidency.
Subscribe to read this story ad-free
Get unlimited access to ad-free articles and exclusive content.
Zelenskyy announced on Telegram that Mykhailo Drapatyi will replace Syrskyi.

Zelenskyy’s decision to fire Fedorov, one of his closest allies, led to rare wartime protests on the streets of Kyiv. Fedorov publicly aired his disagreements with Syrskyi, known as “The Butcher,” over military strategy.

Syrskyi, 60, is a more traditional military commander focused on infantry and artillery, while Fedorov, 35, is seen as a modernizer, whose focus on technological advancements in drone warfare has led to Ukraine’s recent successes in hitting Russia.
Despite the recent shake-up, Zelenskyy tried to present a unified front in his Telegram message Tuesday announcing the dismissal of Syrskyi.
“The desire in all of us is one — victory over the enemy and achieving such conditions on the front and in pressure on Russia, which would allow forcing Russia to peace,” he wrote.

Worried Ukrainians, fearing that Fedorov’s removal could wipe out recent gains, had taken to the streets calling for him to be reinstated and Syrskyi to be forced out, instead. A senior air force commander also quit in protest.

For those in the streets, Syrskyi had become a symbol of the Soviet way of thinking rejected by Ukraine’s younger generations. Fedorov, meanwhile, represents technological innovation and a determination to outsmart the country’s more powerful invader.

Syrskyi has been nicknamed “The Butcher” for his unsparing reputation, with critics pointing to lives lost in a late withdrawal from the fortress city of Bakhmut and the disastrous retreat from Russia’s Kursk region last year that left soldiers stranded and forced to walk back for days under enemy fire.

Zelenskyy spent the weekend speaking to other top military commanders in an apparent interview process to potentially replace Syrskyi. It is unclear whether Fedorov will remain in the government and, if so, in what capacity.

On Tuesday, Zelenskyy separately met with Fedorov and offered him what he called a respected position in government that would unify the country’s technology sector. But it was not clear whether Fedorov accepted the offer and whether the latest moves would satisfy protesters and bring peace to the streets.
“Change is inevitable,” Fedorov said Saturday on social media. “The dialogue is happening. I believe we will succeed.”

Zelenskyy did not give a reason for firing Fedorov last week. He said he was effectively left with a choice between the defense minister and Syrskyi, who was heading the armed forces. The two were no longer communicating with each other, he said.
Fedorov confirmed his spat with Syrskyi, saying Syrskyi was not willing to discuss “problems” directly and resisted reform of Ukraine’s defense apparatus.
Protests erupt in Ukraine over defense minister's ouster
While he credited Syrskyi for Ukraine’s wins in the early days of the war, “the war has changed” because of drone advancements, Fedorov argued.
“Why is this trajectory breaking now, and why are we veering off course? There is such a risk. And the Ukrainian people have taken to the streets for that,” he said at a news conference.

Ukraine’s deployment of low-cost drones has upended the battlefield and the traditional model of warfare, with Kyiv demonstrating a growing ability to hit strategic sites deep inside Russia, in addition to critical Russian-held targets within Ukraine’s territory.

At the same time, Russian troops continue to slowly advance in eastern Ukraine, while a dwindling supply of missile interceptors has left Kyiv and other Ukrainian cities vulnerable to intense bombardment.

title: Andy Burnham becomes seventh British prime minister in a decade
summary: The new Labour Party leader, Andy Burnham, replaced Keir Starmer as British prime minister, inheriting a country beset by low wages and internal strife.
story: LONDON — Over to you, Andy Burnham.
Subscribe to read this story ad-free
Get unlimited access to ad-free articles and exclusive content.

The man dubbed the “King of the North” became the new British prime minister Monday, the latest in a revolving door of leaders trying to halt a decade of political turbulence and economic stagnation in the United Kingdom.
Burnham, 56, was appointed unchallenged after the unpopular Keir Starmer agreed to step down last month following a series of election defeats, U-turns and scandals.

Both Starmer and Burnham come from the same center-left Labour Party, and in the United Kingdom ruling parties can change leaders — and therefore the prime minister — in the middle of an election cycle without anyone voting.
That said, Burnham has promised radical change after taking office following a morning of royal formality, though he already faces infighting over his Cabinet selections.

Burnham reappointed ‌Shabana Mahmood as ​interior ‌minister, but he moved several members of Starmer’s team out of their roles. Former Labour leader Ed Miliband was appointed as foreign minister in place of Yvette Cooper and John Healey became finance minister.
Healey, the former defense minister, helped to trigger the departure of Starmer by accusing him of failing to spend enough money on keeping the country safe.
Making his first speech as prime minister outside No. 10 Downing St., Burnham vowed a “circuit breaker for Britain” that would involve “the biggest changes of the past 40 years.”
In keeping with the more casual style he’s sought to project, Burnham eschewed the lectern favored by his predecessors, instead speaking while standing freely in the famous street.

He said that later this year he would announce a “10-year plan” for Britain, but also that he would be doing things “to give people some breathing space now,” including “some help with the cost of living,” he said. His first “instruction,” Burnham said, would be to “end rough sleeping in our country.”
He said, “I know people at home are fed up with politics. I hear you and I want to be honest with you — we have not been good enough and we need to be better.”
President Donald Trump said he a good call with Burnham on Monday and noted that they would be meeting in the “not too distant future.”

“I had a very good conversation with the new Prime Minister of the United Kingdom, Andy Burnham. We discussed many subjects, including the outstanding relationship we have had with the UK. We will be meeting in the not too distant future for topics of mutual interest,” Trump wrote in a post on X. “The Prime Minister has got a big job ahead of him, but he will be able to do it and, of course, the U.S.A. will be there to help! We discussed North Sea Oil, Trade, the Military Alliance, Demining of the Hormuz Strait, and many other topics. The call was interesting, and went very well. I wished Prime Minister Burnham, GOOD LUCK AND GODSPEED!”

The incoming leader has a heaving inbox: how to solve Britain’s cost-of-living crisis, revive its ailing National Health Service, and navigate bitter debates over immigration and Europe. He must also fend off the challenge from Reform UK, the hard-right party led by Trump ally Nigel Farage, which tops the polls.

title: Tate brothers arrested by U.S. authorities, face additional rape charges in the U.K.
summary: Social media influencers Andrew and Tristan Tate were taken into custody by federal law enforcement officials in Miami on Saturday, the U.S.
story: Social media influencers Andrew and Tristan Tate were taken into custody by federal law enforcement officials in Miami on Saturday, the U.S. Marshals Service said, in arrests British authorities said were related to additional charges of rape.
Subscribe to read this story ad-free
Get unlimited access to ad-free articles and exclusive content.
“We can confirm the arrest of the Tate brothers today in Miami,” it stated. “The warrant was sealed so we are unable to confirm the charges.”

The U.K.’s Crown Prosecution Service said it is bringing additional charges of rape against Andrew, 39, and Tristan, 38, under ongoing cases against the brothers in that nation. The agency said the brothers are awaiting extradition to the U.K.

Andrew Tate faces seven additional counts of rape, three counts of arranging or facilitating trafficking for sexual exploitation, three counts of assault occasioning actual bodily harm and 19 additional charges relating to illegal child images and pornography, the Crown Prosecution Service said.
Tristan Tate faces one count of sexual assault, two counts of rape and three counts of arranging or facilitating trafficking for sexual exploitation, it said.
The allegations cover alleged offenses from July 2010 to August 2017, the service said.

Malcolm McHaffie, head of the Special Crime Division at the Crown Prosecution Service, said in a statement that the charges come after the agency received a new file of evidence from the Bedfordshire Police force.
The new charges relate to four additional alleged victims; previous charges were connected to three alleged victims.
The case against Tristan previously included three counts of rape, six counts of actual bodily harm and two counts of human trafficking.
Tate’s case previously included three counts of rape, four counts of actual bodily harm, two counts of human trafficking and one count of controlling prostitution for gain.
Assistant Chief Constable Karena Thomas of Bedfordshire Police said the complex investigation involved cooperation between “national and international law enforcement agencies.”
She added: “There is no place for male violence against women and girls, and we will continue to work tirelessly to support victims and investigate all reports made to us.”

Joseph D. McBride, a New York City attorney who has been representing the pair in civil litigation, said Saturday that the arrests were an “egregious abuse” of authority by federal officials in the United States.
He said U.K. authorities “conjured up a wave of charges against the Tate brothers” and he predicted the pair would “walk free” before traveling across the Atlantic.
“This is not law enforcement,” he said. “This is a political hit. ... America does not do Britain’s political dirty work.”

On Sunday, McBride said on X that he visited the brothers on Sunday and found them in solitary confinement as they await extradition proceedings. McBride described them as “political prisoners” and “two innocent men, charged with nothing in America, dressed like enemy combatants.”

The brothers, both former kickboxers, are often associated with  the “manosphere,” a social media movement that seeks to elevate men and invalidate feminism, and they have been accused of embodying toxic masculinity and misogyny.
They are dual U.S. and British citizens and moved to Romania in 2016, but amid a criminal investigation there, they returned to the United States last year.
The two have not been convicted of any of the crimes alleged by U.K. or Romanian authorities and have steadfastly denied committing the alleged crimes.

They were arrested along with two Romanian women in Bucharest in 2022 and subsequently indicted. A representative said last year that a Romanian travel ban on the two was lifted, allowing them to return to the United States.

Their return took place in early 2025 as they remained under criminal investigation in Romania on allegations of organized crime, human trafficking, trafficking minors and money laundering. They have denied any wrongdoing.
Speaking last year, attorney McBride said the two planned to travel to Romania to meet with prosecutors there before returning to the U.S.

title: U.S. and Iran trade strikes after two U.S. service members killed in Jordan
summary: Two U.S. service members were killed Friday while defending against an Iranian ballistic missile and drone attack in Jordan, and another service member is missing, U.S.
story: Two U.S. service members were killed Friday while defending against an Iranian ballistic missile and drone attack in Jordan, and another service member is missing, U.S. Central Command said Saturday.
Subscribe to read this story ad-free
Get unlimited access to ad-free articles and exclusive content.

Central Command, known as CENTCOM, said the troops were killed in action as U.S. and partner forces responded to the attack. It did not specify where in Jordan the attack occurred or provide additional details about the circumstances.

Four other American service members were medically evacuated to hospitals in Jordan but have since been discharged, CENTCOM said. Other personnel who were evaluated for minor injuries have returned to duty.
CENTCOM said it was withholding the identities of the two service members killed until 24 hours after their families have been notified.
The U.S. launched retaliatory airstrikes on Saturday at President Donald Trump’s direction in order to “swiftly punish” Iranian forces for the attack, CENTCOM said in a statement.

CENTCOM said that the strikes were also intended to weaken Iran’s “ability to threaten commercial shipping” in the Strait of Hormuz, the latest move by the U.S. to pressure Tehran to give up its control of the critical trade route.

Late Saturday, CENTCOM said U.S. forces completed the eighth consecutive night of launching munitions against Iran, including Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps forces believed to have targeted U.S. service members in Jordan on Friday.
It said U.S. forces struck Iranian military surveillance and air defense facilities, maritime assets and missile and drone storage sites.
The International Atomic Energy Agency said on Sunday that it was investigating reports of an overnight attack on the construction site of Iran’s planned Darkhovin nuclear power plant.

Iran’s semiofficial news agency Tasnim said on Telegram overnight that its own forces had launched “massive drone attacks” on key U.S. military sites in Kuwait and that its attacks would impact U.S. military support operations in the Middle East.
Kuwait’s army said Sunday that its air defenses were “confronting hostile missile and drone attacks.”
The country’s electricity ministry said on X that Iran had attacked a power and water desalination plant twice in two days, causing a fire in part of the facility.

Bahrain, which hosts the U.S. Navy’s 5th Fleet, said Sunday that its air defenses had intercepted an Iranian attack. Its interior ministry said on X that citizens and residents should “remain calm and head to the nearest safe place.”
Jordan’s army forces said it shot down three Iranian missiles targeting the kingdom, according to state television.

The attack that killed U.S. forces comes as the conflict between the U.S. and Iran has intensified following the collapse of an interim ceasefire. The two countries have traded daily strikes over the past week, with Iran launching ballistic missiles and drones at U.S. military positions and American allies across the region, including Jordan, Kuwait and Bahrain, while U.S. forces have carried out repeated strikes on Iranian military targets.

Jordan said earlier Saturday that its forces intercepted Iranian missiles and drones that Tehran said were aimed at an American military base in the country. Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps claimed at least two U.S. fighter jets were destroyed in the attack, according to Iran’s Tasnim news agency. NBC News has not independently verified that claim.

title: Iran and Kuwait report attacks on water and power infrastructure as strikes escalate
summary: Critical water and power infrastructure sites have been damaged as the U.S. and Iran continue to trade strikes, while the parched Middle East reels from temperatures of 100 degrees and beyond.
story: Critical water and power infrastructure sites have been damaged as the U.S. and Iran continue to trade strikes, while the parched Middle East reels from temperatures of 100 degrees and beyond.
Subscribe to read this story ad-free
Get unlimited access to ad-free articles and exclusive content.

Inside Iran, some 10,000 people in 20 villages faced a disrupted water supply on Saturday after the U.S. hit a desalination plant in the Bonji village on the Iranian coast, the semiofficial Tasnim news agency reported, quoting the water company’s chief executive.

“As a result of the attack, the supply of drinking water to several villages in western Jask County has been disrupted,” the Iranian Embassy in India said in a post on X, describing the attack as a war crime.

Iran’s own strikes, primarily aimed at U.S. allies in the region, have repeatedly hit Kuwait this week. The country’s energy ministry on Saturday urged civilians to ration power usage during peak hours after a strike on a power and water desalination plant, causing a fire — the second such attack in two days.
The Kuwait Petroleum Corporation said Saturday that Iran targeted one of its vital sites, causing several injuries and “significant material losses.”

Kuwaiti defense ministry spokesperson Brig. Gen. Saud Al-Otaibi said Saturday there was “severe damage” from strikes on oil and electricity facilities. The country’s foreign ministry meanwhile said that Iran’s targeting of “vital facilities” revealed a “systematic and aggressive approach aimed at civilian targets.”
Energy rationing could prove especially brutal for civilians in Kuwait, who face a scorching summer of over 110 degrees in a relentlessly arid climate.

While the U.S. and Iran have largely traded strikes on military targets since the interim ceasefire agreement collapsed a week ago, the resumed strikes on critical energy infrastructure appear to mark a further escalation.

Iranian Deputy Foreign Minister Kazem Gharibabadi told the semiofficial Fars news agency on Saturday that Iran would follow the U.S. in suspending its commitments under the memorandum of understanding reached last month, adding: “We are no longer implementing them and are focused on defending the country.”
Much of the deal, which stipulated an end to fighting and the free flow of traffic through the Strait of Hormuz, had already been effectively torn up.

U.S. Central Command said late Friday that it had concluded its seventh consecutive night of strikes on military infrastructure and “other assets.” It did not disclose any strikes on civilian infrastructure.

The latest U.S. attacks, and those on bridges linking the critical southern port of Bandar Abbas with the capital Tehran, come as the U.S. seeks to pressure Iran into relinquishing control of the Strait of Hormuz.

The waterway is at the center of the dispute, as Tehran wants ships to move along a route closer to its coast and charge a toll for passage, while Washington has been pushing for a route close to Oman, without Iranian control.

The ceasefire agreement between the two sides has effectively collapsed in recent weeks, with Iran declaring the strait was closed and the U.S. reimposing its naval blockade, effectively bringing shipping traffic to a standstill again after a brief surge.
Since then, the two sides have traded deadly strikes daily.

On Saturday, Kuwait said it had intercepted Iranian missiles and drones and temporarily suspended its airspace, with Kuwait Airways announcing it was rescheduling most of its commercial flights. Iranian missiles were also intercepted by Bahrain on Saturday morning, its defense forces said.

Jordanian forces also intercepted Iranian attacks, which Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps said were aimed at an American base there. At least two U.S. fighter jets were destroyed there, the IRGC said, according to Tasnim on Saturday.
NBC News was unable to verify the claim.
President Donald Trump on Thursday insisted the war was going well, saying in his national address, “We are likewise winning big in Iran.”
“You will see the fruits of that labor very, very shortly.”

Iran said U.S. strikes on its soil, which it says are hitting civilian infrastructure, have killed dozens of people. At least 46 people have been killed and more than 400 injured in the strikes, Iranian officials have said of the recent strikes.
On Friday, Iran also acknowledged strikes on its power infrastructure as its energy ministry issued calls for people to conserve power in the southern provinces, citing “extreme heat.”
Iran also reported strikes on the strategic Qeshm Island and on Friday said that its Chabahar port, where India operates a terminal, was attacked and a control tower was destroyed.
India’s Ministry of External Affairs said Friday that it was aware of the attack but “the terminal itself did not face any damage.”
